precepts.label: Revelation 11:15
precepts.why:
At Jericho it was sevens all the way through: “seven priests shall bear before the ark seven trumpets of rams’ horns: and the seventh day ye shall compass the city seven times, and the priests shall blow with the trumpets.” Six days they went round once, and on the seventh day, the Sabbath day, seven times. “And it came to pass at the seventh time, when the priests blew with the trumpets, Joshua said unto the people, Shout; for the Lord hath given you the city.” Because of their faith, on the seventh day the Most High brought the walls down flat.

Revelation shows the same pattern at the end: “And the seventh angel sounded; and there were great voices in heaven, saying, The kingdoms of this world are become the kingdoms of our Lord, and of his Christ; and he shall reign for ever and ever.” The seventh angel sounded the trump, and that brought forth completion. It is the same thing that happened when our forefathers walked around the walls of Jericho.

Seven represents completion and totality, and it also represents complete deliverance. Nothing is accidental with the Most High; he uses seven as a form of deliverance. From the beginning it has been there: the seventh day rest, Naaman dipped seven times, and Jericho compassed seven times by seven priests with seven trumpets.

So the seventh trumpet at Jericho gave Israel the city, and the seventh trumpet in Revelation gives the kingdoms of this world to our Lord and his Christ. All of this is a representation of Christ, and it points to the complete deliverance of Israel when he reigns.

precepts.label: 1 Samuel 16:13
precepts.why:
David was anointed more than once, and it starts here in Bethlehem: “Then Samuel took the horn of oil, and anointed him in the midst of his brethren: and the Spirit of the Lord came upon David from that day forward.” Samuel anointed him in the midst of his brethren, and the Spirit of the Lord stayed on him from that day.

After Saul was dead, David went up to the cities of Hebron, and the men of Judah came and anointed David king over the house of Judah. So he was anointed again in Hebron, but only over Judah; he was the king of Judah in Hebron.

Then all the tribes came: “Then came all the tribes of Israel to David unto Hebron, and spake, saying, Behold, we are thy bone and thy flesh.” They remembered that “when Saul was king over us, thou wast he that leddest out and broughtest in Israel”, and that the Lord had said, “Thou shalt feed my people Israel, and thou shalt be a captain over Israel.” So “they anointed David king over Israel.” Now he is king over all twelve. “In Hebron he reigned over Judah seven years and six months: and in Jerusalem he reigned thirty and three years over all Israel and Judah”: both kingdoms. And “David took the strong hold of Zion: the same is the city of David.” Zion is the city of David.

But the beef was already there before the split. In 2 Samuel 19 the men of Israel asked, “Why have our brethren the men of Judah stolen thee away”; Judah answered, “Because the king is near of kin to us”: he is our tribe. Israel said, “We have ten parts in the king, and we have also more right in David than ye”: there are more of us than you, why can't we anoint him over here? “And the words of the men of Judah were fiercer than the words of the men of Israel.” Judah cursed Ephraim out, and that enmity between the two stayed.

Ephraim felt more entitled, and in a way rightfully so: Joseph saved Israel from starvation in Egypt, Joshua of Ephraim brought us into the land and gave out the allotments, and Ephraim held Shiloh, Bethel and the first places of worship. So the anointing that began in the midst of David's brethren is also where the dividing hatred between Judah and Ephraim shows itself, a rivalry that went on long after David.

precepts.label: Sirach 47:23
precepts.why:
Solomon fell in love with heathen women, the very nations of which the Lord said “Ye shall not go in to them, neither shall they come in unto you: for surely they will turn away your heart after their gods”, and they did. He built a high place for Chemosh for his Moabite wife and for Molech for his Ammonite wife, and did the same for all his strange wives. So the Lord was angry with Solomon, and the prophet Ahijah “rent it in twelve pieces” and told Jeroboam, “Take thee ten pieces”: the kingdom would be rent out of the hand of Solomon’s son, with one tribe left for David’s sake.

Sirach sums up what Solomon left behind him when he died: “Thus rested Solomon with his fathers, and of his seed he left behind him Roboam, even the foolishness of the people, and one that had no understanding, who turned away the people through his counsel.” Rehoboam was an idiot. He did not listen to the elders; he listened to the friends he grew up with, and by his counsel he turned the people away.

“There was also Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who caused Israel to sin, and shewed Ephraim the way of sin”. Jeroboam, the mighty man of valor Solomon made ruler over the house of Joseph, plotted against Solomon to rush the prophecy, fled to Egypt, and came back to take the ten tribes. And he showed Ephraim the way of sin.

So the heart Solomon gave to his strange wives bore its fruit in the next generation: a foolish son on the throne of Judah, a king who led Ephraim into sin, and the kingdom divided in two. That is where the dividing hatred between the houses begins.

precepts.label: 2 Chronicles 36:16
precepts.why:
Elijah cries that the children of Israel have “thrown down thine altars, and slain thy prophets with the sword; and I, even I only, am left”. They made a covenant with death and hell. The prophets taught against the rulers and their falsehoods, so the rulers killed the prophets. Chronicles shows how it went all the way to the end of the kingdom.

“But they mocked the messengers of God”: that is what they do now. Look at how they mock the purple and gold, calling us purple Power Rangers. It is the same thing; they mocked us. “and despised his words”: despised his law, like they do now. “and misused his prophets”: had them locked up, exiled, or killed in terrible ways.

“until the wrath of the Lord arose against his people, till there was no remedy.” They pissed the Lord off until there was no remedy left. The killing of the prophets Elijah complained of was not one king’s sin; it was the way of the nation until the wrath came.

precepts.label: Susanna 1:5
precepts.why:
Who were the rulers who killed the prophets? The history of Susanna shows where their wickedness came from. “There dwelt a man in Babylon, called Joacim”, a great rich man with a fair garden, “and to him resorted the Jews; because he was more honourable than all others.” He was an elder, a leader, and the people came to sit with him.

“The same year were appointed two of the ancients of the people to be judges, such as the Lord spake of, that wickedness came from Babylon from ancient judges, who seemed to govern the people.” We had ancient judges in Babylon, and they brought Babylonian doctrine and ideals along with them. They seemed to govern the people, but they were not true governors; they were evil and wicked as hell.

These same elders who came out of Babylon, and whose line made its way down to the time of Roman rule, started the Talmud. The Babylonian Talmud: they got it from Babylon. So when Christ condemned their traditions, those traditions came from Babylon. These are the fathers of the Pharisees, the same spirit of the rulers who slew the prophets.

precepts.label: Jeremiah 29:21-23
precepts.why:
Susanna says wickedness came from Babylon from ancient judges, “such as the Lord spake of”. Where did the Lord speak of it? In Jeremiah, to “all ye of the captivity, whom I have sent from Jerusalem to Babylon”.

“Thus saith the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, of Ahab the son of Kolaiah, and of Zedekiah the son of Maaseiah, which prophesy a lie unto you in my name; Behold, I will deliver them into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon; and he shall slay them before your eyes”. And the captivity would curse by their names: “The Lord make thee like Zedekiah and like Ahab, whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire”. He cooked them to death.

Why? “Because they have committed villany in Israel, and have committed adultery with their neighbours’ wives, and have spoken lying words in my name, which I have not commanded them”. That is what your pastors be doing. “even I know, and am a witness, saith the Lord.”

These were the wicked leaders among the people, false prophets instead of the true ones they persecuted. The Pharisees did the exact same thing when Rome ruled: ancient evil from Babylon, from the elders.

precepts.label: 2 Esdras 1:32-35
precepts.why:
The Lord says it through Ezra: “I sent unto you my servants the prophets, whom ye have taken and slain, and torn their bodies in pieces, whose blood I will require of your hands, saith the Lord.” We were doing it to each other. We were killing the prophets of our own people, and he will require that blood.

“Thus saith the Almighty Lord, Your house is desolate, I will cast you out as the wind doth stubble. And your children shall not be fruitful; for they have despised my commandment, and done the thing that is an evil before me.”

“Your houses will I give to a people that shall come; which not having heard of me yet shall believe me; to whom I have shewed no signs, yet they shall do that I have commanded them.” That is us today. We are born again.

Christ said the same in the parable of the vineyard: the husbandmen beat one servant, killed another and stoned another, and last of all killed the son, and the lord of the vineyard “will miserably destroy those wicked men, and will let out his vineyard unto other husbandmen”. The other husbandmen are us today, the people Ezra spoke of. “The kingdom of God shall be taken from you, and given to a nation bringing forth the fruits thereof.”

precepts.label: Matthew 23:37-38
precepts.why:
Christ says it to the city: “O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee”. Over and over again, the same thing Elijah cried about: they slew the prophets.

“how often would I have gathered thy children together”: gathered both kingdoms together, “even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not!” They refused him, the stone which the builders refused.

“Behold, your house is left unto you desolate.” These are the same words the Lord spoke through Ezra, “Your house is desolate”. The rulers who killed the prophets would kill the Son too, and their house would be left empty, cast out as the wind doth stubble.

precepts.label: Acts 7:51-54
precepts.why:
Stephen prophesied against the rulers, the builders of his time: “Ye stiffnecked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, ye do always resist the Holy Ghost: as your fathers did, so do ye.” As your fathers did, so do you.

“Which of the prophets have not your fathers persecuted? and they have slain them which shewed before of the coming of the Just One”. The prophets were killed in the Old Testament, and who were they prophesying of? The Just One. So when the prophets prophesied of a Messiah, they were killed. The killers who got away with it had children, and their children knew who they had killed. Then when Christ was born, they killed him too: “of whom ye have been now the betrayers and murderers: Who have received the law by the disposition of angels, and have not kept it.”

“When they heard these things, they were cut to the heart, and they gnashed on him with their teeth.” Why cut to the heart? Because they knew. Stephen was in the spirit; he saw their fathers killing the prophets: your father killed Zechariah, your father killed Isaiah. They knew and did not care, and they were pissed off that he said it. They gnashed on him, cursing him out.

The prophets were sent to bring us back to God, and the rulers hated them because the prophets could see right through them. It was the same spirit in Elijah’s day, in Christ’s day, and in Rome against the apostles, and it is the same spirit today.

thread.label: 2 Kings 5:10-14
thread.text: And Elisha sent a messenger unto him, saying, Go and wash in Jordan seven times, and thy flesh shall come again to thee, and thou shalt be clean.

classes.title: 70 Times 7: The Perfection of Mercy Through Christ

precepts.label: Isaiah 1:16-20
precepts.why:
Naaman was told, “Wash, and be clean”, and when he believed and obeyed the word of the prophet, he was clean. Isaiah shows what the true washing is: “Wash you, make you clean; put away the evil of your doings from before mine eyes; cease to do evil; Learn to do well”.

Put away the evil of your doings: that's the true washing. Cease to do evil, learn to do well. Action, action, action. Not speak well, do well. “seek judgment, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow.”

“though your sins be as scarlet”, bloodshot red, “they shall be as white as snow”, if you learn to do well. “though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool.” But it hangs on obedience: “If ye be willing and obedient, ye shall eat the good of the land: But if ye refuse and rebel, ye shall be devoured with the sword”.

That is Naaman. At first he refused and went away in a rage. When he humbled himself and did according to the saying of the man of God, his flesh came again like the flesh of a little child. His belief and his obedience are what made him clean.

precepts.label: Psalms 51:6-7
precepts.why:
Naaman believed that the word of the prophet would heal him if he followed the commandment, going down to the river Jordan and dipping seven times. That belief is what healed him of his leprosy.

David prays the same way: “Behold, thou desirest truth in the inward parts: and in the hidden part thou shalt make me to know wisdom.” Truth in the inward parts is what the Most High desires. Then: “Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean: wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow.”

The water of the Jordan did not do it by itself; the Jordan was muddy water, and Naaman would rather have had the rivers of Damascus. The word of God is what really cleanses us of our sins. Naaman obeyed the word, and he was made clean, his flesh like the flesh of a little child.

precepts.label: Luke 3:3-4
precepts.why:
We read about Naaman going down into the river Jordan to be cleansed. Luke brings us back to that same river: John “came into all the country about Jordan, preaching the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins; As it is written in the book of the words of Esaias the prophet, saying, The voice of one crying in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make his paths straight.”

The baptism of repentance, for the remission of sins, preached about Jordan. Naaman was washed of his leprosy in the Jordan, and John preached the washing away of sins in the same Jordan. Nothing is accidental with the Most High.

It was Christ who healed Naaman, working through Elisha by his spirit. And John in the Jordan was preparing the way of that same Lord.

precepts.label: Matthew 3:13
precepts.why:
“Then cometh Jesus from Galilee to Jordan unto John, to be baptized of him.” Christ went unto John the Baptist to be baptized, and in what river? Jordan: the same river that Naaman had to dip in seven times.

Seven represents completion. Naaman dipped seven times in Jordan, completion in the river Jordan, and his flesh came again like the flesh of a little child. The number and the river both point to the same Christ.

Who did the healing for Naaman? Not Elisha on his own. Elisha was working by the spirit of Christ; Christ is the one who did the healing, and he used Elisha as the prophet. So when Christ himself comes to the Jordan, it is the same one who cleansed Naaman there, the one who makes us clean.

precepts.label: Luke 4:25-27
precepts.why:
Christ himself reached back and referenced this exact history. “I tell you of a truth, many widows were in Israel in the days of Elias, when the heaven was shut up three years and six months, when great famine was throughout all the land; But unto none of them was Elias sent, save unto Sarepta, a city of Sidon, unto a woman that was a widow.”

Then the point: “And many lepers were in Israel in the time of Eliseus the prophet; and none of them was cleansed, saving Naaman the Syrian.” Of all the lepers, the one cleansed was the one who humbled himself, believed, and went down and dipped seven times according to the saying of the man of God.

And seven also represents complete deliverance. Naaman dipped seven times and was delivered from his leprosy; Christ, the one whose spirit healed him through Elisha, spoke of it himself.

precepts.label: 2 Kings 17:1
precepts.why:
“In the twelfth year of Ahaz king of Judah began Hoshea the son of Elah to reign in Samaria over Israel nine years”. Ahaz, wicked and weak, was over Judah, and Hoshea was over Ephraim, the northern kingdom. Hoshea “did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord, but not as the kings of Israel that were before him”.

“Against him came up Shalmaneser king of Assyria”. This is Pul’s son. In 1 Chronicles 5 it was Pul, Tiglath-pileser, who came first and took Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh; now his son Shalmaneser comes and does the most. The northern kingdom was not taken all at once. It was done in waves: one group taken out here, some of Reuben, some of Asher there, until almost all of Ephraim was out of the land.

Hoshea became his servant and paid him, then conspired against him: “he had sent messengers to So king of Egypt, and brought no present to the king of Assyria”. He tried to align himself with Egypt to defy Assyria, so the king of Assyria bound him in prison, “went up to Samaria, and besieged it three years”, and “carried Israel away into Assyria, and placed them in Halah and in Habor by the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes”. That is modern day Iran, bordering Russia. From there our people kept migrating further and further east: the northern kingdom became Scythians, moving from Iran into Russia, some as far as China, some as far as Japan, where they became samurai.

Why it happened: “the children of Israel had sinned against the Lord their God”, and they “did secretly those things that were not right”. They thought God wasn’t watching; he saw it all. They built high places in every city, “rejected his statutes, and his covenant”, “followed vanity, and became vain, and went after the heathen”. So “the Lord was very angry with Israel, and removed them out of his sight: there was none left but the tribe of Judah only”. Yet “Judah kept not the commandments” either, and “the Lord rejected all the seed of Israel”. God was done with all twelve: the northern kingdom into captivity, and Judah next.

Then the land was filled with heathen: “the king of Assyria brought men from Babylon, and from Cuthah, and from Ava, and from Hamath, and from Sepharvaim, and placed them in the cities of Samaria instead of the children of Israel”. The Lord sent lions to kill them for their evil, so a priest was brought back to teach them “the manner of the God of the land”, how to sacrifice so they could stay in the land in Ephraim’s absence. “Howbeit every nation made gods of their own, and put them in the houses of the high places which the Samaritans had made”. The northern kingdom was called Samaritans because Samaria was their capital, and these heathen sacrificed in the very high places Ephraim made for their idols. And “the men of Babylon made Succoth–benoth, and the men of Cuth made Nergal, and the men of Hamath made Ashima”.

So the carrying away in 1 Chronicles 5:26 was the start of this: God himself stirred up the kings of Assyria against the tribes that went whoring after other gods, and the northern kingdom was broken and scattered, with strangers set in their place.

precepts.label: 2 Chronicles 19:5
precepts.why:
“Now for a long season Israel hath been without the true God, and without a teaching priest, and without law.” That is the northern kingdom: they stopped going to Jerusalem to worship, and Jeroboam set up idols for them. So when Asa gathered “all Judah and Benjamin, and the strangers with them out of Ephraim and Manasseh, and out of Simeon”, the northern tribes are called strangers. And “they fell to him out of Israel in abundance, when they saw that the Lord his God was with him.” Whenever Judah was on point, Ephraim would follow along.

The next king shows the same thing. Jehoshaphat, a good king of Judah, reigned from 870 to 848 BC. “And Jehoshaphat dwelt at Jerusalem: and he went out again through the people from Beer–sheba to mount Ephraim, and brought them back unto the Lord God of their fathers.” Who dwelt at Beersheba? Simeon: that was Simeon’s allotment of land. From Simeon’s land all the way to mount Ephraim, Jehoshaphat caused some of Ephraim to return back to the Lord.

“And he set judges in the land throughout all the fenced cities of Judah, city by city, And said to the judges, Take heed what ye do: for ye judge not for man, but for the Lord, who is with you in the judgment.” “Wherefore now let the fear of the Lord be upon you; take heed and do it: for there is no iniquity with the Lord our God, nor respect of persons, nor taking of gifts.” Jehoshaphat was a righteous king, and he set the law back in place.

So Israel was without God, without a teaching priest and without law, and the Lord would always use Judah to bring Ephraim back in, every single time. When Judah was on point, Ephraim followed along; when Judah went off, Ephraim went even worse off.

precepts.label: Ezekiel 8:14
precepts.why:
Manasseh “caused his children to pass through the fire in the valley of the son of Hinnom”. That valley, Gehenna, was where Israel burned its garbage, our refuse; the Muslims call it Gehenna, their hell. Where garbage used to be burned, they burned their children, in honor of Baal.

There was an order to it. In the spring they held orgies in honor of Ashtoreth, the fertility goddess, a black Hamite deity whose star is Venus and whose nose is knocked off the statues. Everyone slept with everyone, and the women got pregnant. Nine months later, in the winter, came the bull god, Baal, the sun god the Egyptians called Apis. The babies were laid on the plates of the brass bull with a fire under it and around it; as they burned they wiggled off into the flame, and drums were beaten to drown out their screams. That is what Manasseh was doing, by the thousands. Carnival babies, Freaknik and the club today are the same worship of that goddess.

Why sacrifice the babies? Ashtoreth gave birth to a baby god, Tammuz, and Tammuz died as an infant. The same way she lost her child, the women had to lose theirs, and the same way she wept for her child, they had to weep for the children they sacrificed on the altar. That is why Jesus is always pictured as a baby with Mary.

Ezekiel saw it: “Then he brought me to the door of the gate of the Lord’s house which was toward the north; and, behold, there sat women weeping for Tammuz.” That is what they had to do once they were in that idolatry: weep for the babies they themselves had sacrificed. And it was worse than what is brought out here.

precepts.label: Wisdom of Solomon 12:3-7
precepts.why:
“So Manasseh made Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem to err, and to do worse than the heathen, whom the Lord had destroyed before the children of Israel.” Worse than the nations we were killing out of the land for doing the exact same thing. What does that mean? Wisdom of Solomon gives an idea.

“For it was thy will to destroy by the hands of our fathers both those old inhabitants of thy holy land”. Our fathers were Joshua, Caleb and the elders who succeeded Moses; when we entered the promised land we had to war with the nations already there. The old inhabitants were the Canaanites, the Hamites living in the land before we got there.

“Whom thou hatedst for doing most odious works of witchcrafts, and wicked sacrifices”: odious works are filth, evil, vile things, and that is what Manasseh was doing. “And also those merciless murderers of children”: Manasseh did it and had the people do it. “and devourers of man’s flesh, and the feasts of blood”: cannibalism, drinking blood, eating flesh. Who knows what Manasseh was doing, but he was worse than the heathen, so we have to factor this in. “and the parents, that killed with their own hands souls destitute of help”: we were killing our own kids.

“That the land, which thou esteemedst above all other, might receive a worthy colony of God’s children.” The Lord had us go in and kill those nations out of the land because they were doing these things. Then we got the land, turned around, and did the exact same thing and worse under Manasseh, as Ahab did in his time. Manasseh was one of the worst kings Judah ever had.

precepts.label: Sirach 6:17-18
precepts.why:
“The law of the Lord is perfect, converting the soul.” The law of God is perfect, it is pure, there is nothing wrong with it, and converting means to change. Only the law can change you. I used to be a murderer; the law said thou shalt not murder. I used to be a thief; the law said thou shalt not steal. I used to be an abuser. Once I know the Lord, I repent. Same thing, brother. Same thing, sister, with your trauma. Stop using your trauma as a crutch. It happened when you were 14, 15, 16, and now you're 46, 50, in your third marriage, still using it, and you can't keep a man or a woman because you cannot cope.

We never grew up around order, structure and unity. So when we come around it now, we begin to feel uncomfortable, because we realize we are the problem: the reason environments become toxic, the reason people bicker and fight, the instigating spirit we grew up seeing. Now, in a body and a truth where the light shines on that, you are forced to change, and brothers and sisters do not want to.

“Whoso feareth the Lord shall direct his friendship aright: for as he is, so shall his neighbour be also.” If you fear the Lord, you are going to direct your friendships aright, because as you are, so shall your neighbour be. But if you are constantly having issues, constantly having problems, who is the issue? Who is causing these troubles? With the laws of God and all the examples in the scriptures, you should be able to direct your friendship aright. So why is your name always in something?

“My son, gather instruction from thy youth up: so shalt thou find wisdom till thine old age.” We didn't have the opportunity to gather instruction from our youth up. But coming into this truth we have to be born again and begin to do so. You can't drag in all the ways your grandmama and your auntie and them used to deal with each other. It's a new day.

precepts.label: Sirach 6:20-21
precepts.why:
“She is very unpleasant to the unlearned.” Wisdom is very unpleasant to the unlearned. You didn't learn about yourself. All you ever did was point out other people's problems. You never examined yourself; you never looked in the mirror. So now that wisdom finally reveals who you are, it is very unpleasant.

“he that is without understanding will not remain with her.” That's why people have to find a reason to leave. They get offended, they find a reason to be mad, and then they go. What is the root cause? They don't want to change once that wisdom is revealed. And the law, which is perfect, converts only the soul that will be changed.

Destructive attitudes begin internally before they become visible externally. A person may still attend services, teach, lead, pray or serve while harboring the wrong spirit, an evil spirit. You look at the fringes and think, he's good, she's good; you would be surprised how many have an evil spirit in the midst of us. Some come here to destroy the unity of the brotherhood, because in the world it's always chaos: you never see a room full of black people with no fight, no argument, breaking bread together. Whatever you were going through in the world, you had better get over it, and quick, because that thing will destroy you. Those who carry that spirit will find themselves outside these doors.

precepts.label: Psalms 51:17
precepts.why:
David says it plainly: “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise.” A sacrifice for the Lord is not so much an animal. What he wants laid on the altar is a broken spirit, a broken and contrite heart, which is a broken mind.

That is the same thing Psalms 34:18 says: “The Lord is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart.” Man by nature is arrogant; we do what we want to do. So the Most High will put you in a position where he has to break you, break you down and shame you, bring you down to the lowest, until you realize: I can't do these things no more, I have to humble myself and do better, for the Lord's sake first and foremost, for my own sake, and for my people's sake as an example.

Isaiah shows where the Lord dwells when he comes near. “the high and lofty One that inhabiteth eternity” is the Father, and eternity is his domain, the upper room, the top floor. Yet he says, “I dwell in the high and holy place, with him also that is of a contrite and humble spirit, to revive the spirit of the humble, and to revive the heart of the contrite ones.” The Father and his Son deal with and dwell with the humble in spirit.

That broken spirit is the sacrifice worthy of his time. Being haughty and arrogant and offering the best sacrifices is a complete waste of time, because humility comes before honor. That is how Manasseh, a man the law said should die, found mercy: he humbled himself, and God would not despise that broken heart.

precepts.label: 1 Samuel 15:22
precepts.why:
Psalms 51:16: “For thou desirest not sacrifice; else would I give it: thou delightest not in burnt offering.” David is saying, you don’t desire sacrifice, otherwise I would give it to you; you don’t care about that either. The Lord revealed to David, I don’t care about sacrifices. And Saul didn’t listen either.

“And Samuel said, Hath the Lord as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the Lord?” Samuel is asking the question: does the Lord require sacrifices above obeying what he tells you to do?

“Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams.” To hearken is to listen and humble yourself. That is better than the fat of rams.

So “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise.” The sacrifice God accepts is a broken spirit. The animals were just temporary; your mind being broken and humbled is the best sacrifice the Lord desires. You can offer and sacrifice all you want, but make sure you offer with a good heart. “Then shalt thou be pleased with the sacrifices of righteousness, with burnt offering and whole burnt offering: then shall they offer bullocks upon thine altar.” Once the sacrifices of righteousness are offered, then the bullocks on the altar become acceptable.

precepts.label: Sirach 35:17
precepts.why:
Psalms 51:17 says “a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise.” Ecclesiasticus 35:17 shows what happens when the humbled one prays.

“The prayer of the humble pierceth the clouds.” It pierces the clouds: the Lord hears it. “And till it come nigh, he will not be comforted; and will not depart, till the most High shall behold to judge righteously, and execute judgment.”

That is David in Psalms 51. When Nathan confronted him after Bathsheba and Uriah, he did not stay the smartest guy in the room. He said, you are right, I am guilty: “For I acknowledge my transgressions: and my sin is ever before me.” He kept the promise he made in Psalms 32:5, “I acknowledged my sin unto thee, and mine iniquity have I not hid.” He held himself accountable, and you have to hold yourself accountable when it comes to your sins.

The bones that were broken were his humbling: being confronted with his wrong, confessing it and acknowledging it, and the consequences that followed. And out of that broken, humbled place he prayed, “Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.” That is the prayer of the humble, the one that pierces the clouds, and it is the same humility that brought mercy to King Manasseh.

precepts.label: Micah 3:5-6
precepts.why:
“The stone which the builders refused” is refused by the builders, the rulers, because they were in darkness. Micah shows the darkness God put on them: “Thus saith the Lord concerning the prophets that make my people err, that bite with their teeth, and cry, Peace; and he that putteth not into their mouths, they even prepare war against him.” They prepare war against us, because they are teaching the wrong thing.

“Therefore night shall be unto you”. He is talking to the prophets, the elders. Night goes back to darkness, your eyes being closed. If you can't see, you start stumbling; you don't know where you're going, you're falling. That is the stone of stumbling at work.

It goes on, “that ye shall not have a vision”: your eyes are closed, you can't read the Bible no more, you can't teach the Bible no more. God stops talking to you entirely. Then “it shall be dark unto you, that ye shall not divine”: you cannot teach correctly. So now you go to theology school and run to the white man for help: Mr. White Man, can you teach me the Bible, please? Can I go to your school and learn BS, please?

Then “the sun shall go down over the prophets, and the day shall be dark over them.” The sun going down means dark: no understanding. The light is taken from them and they lose understanding.

That is why the builders refused the stone. And it was the Lord's doing: the builders rejecting him so that they would have him killed, and so bring in the northern kingdom, whereunto they were appointed. Not all Israel refused him; the builders did. And he that was refused “is become the head stone of the corner”: he becomes our king and ruler in the end.

precepts.label: Proverbs 8:22-23
precepts.why:
“Wisdom hath builded her house”. Who is this wisdom? Go back a chapter, where wisdom speaks: “The Lord possessed me in the beginning of his way, before his works of old. I was set up from everlasting, from the beginning, or ever the earth was.”

This is going into Christ and wisdom, one and the same, interchangeable. Christ is the ultimate wisdom, the complete wisdom, set up from everlasting before the earth was.

That is why chapter 9 says wisdom “hath hewn out her seven pillars”. Seven represents completion, and Christ is complete wisdom. The house wisdom built stands on him, the one the Lord possessed in the beginning of his way.

precepts.label: Isaiah 11:1-2
precepts.why:
Wisdom “hath hewn out her seven pillars”. Let's see who this wisdom pertains to and who had these seven pillars. Isaiah: “And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots”. That is talking about Christ.

Now count what rests upon him. “And the spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him”: that's one. “the spirit of wisdom”: two. “and understanding”: three. “the spirit of counsel”: four. “And might”: five. “the spirit of knowledge”: six. “and of the fear of the Lord”: seven.

Those are the seven pillars of wisdom that Christ had. Seven represents completion, so they represent complete spiritual perfection, and that is what Christ operated in. Wisdom's house on seven pillars is Christ, full of the spirit of the Lord in every part.

precepts.label: 1 John 1:9
precepts.why:
“He that covereth his sins shall not prosper”: when you try to cover that bitterness, the roots keep growing, and you are just bringing in dump trucks to load more soil on top of it. But whoso confesses shall have mercy, and John shows why: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins”. The Lord is faithful and just when we confess our sins.

That goes all the way back to Leviticus. When you brought your sacrifice before the priest, that was a public confession. You had to walk through the midst of all Israel with your offering.

Now we have the white man, his walls and his technology. We have VPNs: yeah, don't nobody know I'm on OnlyFans, I got a VPN, I'm broadcasting from the Philippines. No, brother, the Lord sees right through it.

So in order to get over the root of bitterness we have to confess it: damn, I had the devil on me. Covering it will never prosper; confessing it is how we get the mercy we all want.

precepts.label: James 5:16
precepts.why:
Confessing is not only to the Lord. James says: “Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed. The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much.”

We should be comfortable confessing our faults, because, as 1 Corinthians 10:13 says, no temptation has taken you but such as is common to man. You confess your fault, and a brother might say, brother, I was dealing with the same spirit. Woo, man, I feel a lot better. All of this is common. We all have levels of bitterness; some have a higher degree than others, but everybody deals with a level of bitterness, a level of lust, a level of lack of faith.

That doesn't mean getting on the public announcement. It means you see a godly man and say, hey Cap, hey D, I have this going on, I need help with it. They are going to help you. They are not going to say, brother, you got the devil on you, get away from me. It is Satan telling us otherwise.

That is whoso confesseth and forsaketh: confessing to the Lord, confessing one to another, and being healed, instead of covering the sin and letting the root grow.

precepts.label: Matthew 11:28
precepts.why:
Isaiah calls us “a people laden with iniquity.” Christ answers that very word: “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” Heavy laden with what? With sin, the iniquity Isaiah just named.

That is why we are in need of a saviour. We read the history of our forefathers in the wilderness: the Most High showed great signs and wonders, and we were still a stiff-necked, hard-headed people. We are “a sinful nation”, “a seed of evildoers, children that are corrupters.” We forsake the Lord every time we sin, and we have “provoked the Holy One of Israel unto anger.” That is why the so-called blacks and Hispanics went into captivity, just as Deuteronomy 28:15 through 68 laid out the curses for breaking the commandments. Many of our brothers and sisters are still going backward, moonwalking away from the Most High. Brothers and sisters, we cannot do it without Christ.

So be honest and sincere, even in prayer. Do not go to the Most High acting righteous when you are full of dead bones, sin and guile. None of us is righteous; we are trying, but there is sin still in us. Open your mouth and confess the things you are battling with.

“and I will give you rest.” That rest is not a good night’s sleep. It is our land, the kingdom of God, rulership for a thousand years under Christ. That is the true rest he is talking about, but we have to come unto him. Now is our time to get our minds right and repent.

precepts.label: Isaiah 8:14
precepts.why:
In the days of Ahaz, Ephraim conspired with the Syrians to overthrow Judah: the Syro-Ephraimite war. Rezin was the king of Syria and Pekah the son of Remaliah was king of Ephraim, and their plan was to take Judah's land and set the son of Tabeal as king over it. Ahaz was weak and wicked, and his heart shook “as the trees of the wood are moved”. But the Lord said the counsel of Syria and Ephraim would not stand: “within threescore and five years shall Ephraim be broken, that it be not a people.”

In Isaiah 8 the Lord brings “the king of Assyria, and all his glory” like a river over his banks. Assyria would rise up and conquer Ephraim, and also pass through Judah and take some portions of it, but not fully like Ephraim. “Take counsel together, and it shall come to nought” … “for God is with us.” Isaiah's sons were born as signs that Ephraim and Syria would be overthrown by Assyria and would not succeed against Judah.

So the Lord tells Isaiah not to fear their confederacy, and not to be like Ahaz, cowardly and weak: “Sanctify the Lord of hosts himself; and let him be your fear, and let him be your dread. And he shall be for a sanctuary; but for a stone of stumbling and for a rock of offence to both the houses of Israel.” It says both. The Lord speaks of one Israel as two houses: the house of Judah and the house of Ephraim, the southern kingdom and the northern kingdom. And that stone of stumbling is Christ.

He is “for a gin and for a snare to the inhabitants of Jerusalem”, a trap to both houses, but specifically to those in Jerusalem. “And many among them shall stumble, and fall, and be broken, and be snared, and be taken.” The context has not changed. Not only did Ephraim fall physically and spiritually; Judah fell physically and spiritually too, but worse, because they stumbled at that stone.

Hosea shows Ephraim's side. His daughter Lo-ruhamah, no mercy: “I will no more have mercy upon the house of Israel; but I will utterly take them away”, which is Assyria overthrowing Ephraim so that it be not a people. His son Lo-ammi: “for ye are not my people, and I will not be your God.” When you are not God's people and he is not your God, that makes you a Gentile, a heathen, a stranger, a non-Israelite. Judah read that and said, good, the hell with Ephraim, they are Gentiles, we don't deal with them anymore.

The rock ties it together. Moses said “He is the Rock, his work is perfect” … “a God of truth and without iniquity”, and “is not he thy father that hath bought thee?” That rock of Isaiah 8 is Christ, our God and our father, and the stone both houses of Israel stumbled over.

thread.label: Isaiah 7:8
thread.text: For the head of Syria is Damascus, and the head of Damascus is Rezin; and within threescore and five years shall Ephraim be broken, that it be not a people.

classes.title: The Dividing Hatred: the Grafted in Strangers

precepts.label: Sirach 50:25-26
precepts.why:
Ephraim aligned itself with Syria to attack its own brother Judah, and Isaiah 7:8 is the prophecy against them for it. “For the head of Syria is Damascus”, Syria's capital, “and the head of Damascus is Rezin”, the king of the Syrians at that time, “and within threescore and five years shall Ephraim be broken, that it be not a people.” That is who Moses was talking about when he said the Lord would provoke Israel to jealousy with them which are not a people, with a foolish nation: Ephraim.

Sirach shows the same people by name and place. “There be two manner of nations which my heart abhorreth, and the third is no nation.” Two nations he despises, and the third is no nation at all. “They that sit upon the mountain of Samaria”: in this context that is the Greeks, who ruled over Samaria then, and he says he despises them. “And they that dwell among the Philistines”: the Philistines are Hamites, and he hates them too.

“And that foolish people that dwell in Sichem.” Foolish, and no nation: the very words Moses used, not a people and foolish. Who dwelt in Shechem? The northern kingdom. Shechem is in Samaria, northern kingdom's land, where Abraham built that altar. It is by Sychar, where Christ met the woman at the well, near “the parcel of ground that Jacob gave to his son Joseph”, the land of Ephraim and Manasseh.

So Isaiah says Ephraim would be broken that it be not a people, Hosea calls them Lo-ammi, not my people, and Sirach calls them no nation and foolish. It is the same people every time. And that is why Peter writes to “the strangers scattered” which “in time past were not a people, but are now the people of God”: Christ laid down his life for the other sheep not of Judah's fold, to gather together in one the children of God that were scattered abroad.

precepts.label: 2 Chronicles 34:9
precepts.why:
Under Josiah, when the money for the house of God was brought to Hilkiah the high priest, it was “the money that was brought into the house of God, which the Levites that kept the doors had gathered of the hand of Manasseh and Ephraim, and of all the remnant of Israel, and of all Judah and Benjamin”.

Manasseh donated toward the temple in Jerusalem, and Ephraim donated too. Why “the remnant of Israel”? Because Assyria had taken most of them out of the land in waves; remnants remained, some idolatrous and some faithful. And that was during Josiah’s reign: whenever Judah is on point, Ephraim follows along.

Then Isaiah speaks to those same northern lands: “the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali”, afflicted “by the way of the sea, beyond Jordan, in Galilee of the nations.” Zebulun came to keep the Passover in Hezekiah’s day, and Tobit was of Naphtali. Galilee of the Gentiles is where the northern kingdom resided, and they were called Gentiles. “The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light”: the people of verse 1, the northern kingdom.

“For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given”: unto us, not all. He is the Prince of Peace because he must bring peace between those who have hatred for each other, so that there is no more division between the two kingdoms. “The Lord sent a word into Jacob, and it hath lighted upon Israel. And all the people shall know, even Ephraim and the inhabitant of Samaria”. The same Ephraim and Manasseh whose remnant gave to the house of God in Judah’s good days would see the light of the son born of Judah.

precepts.label: Isaiah 27:12-13
precepts.why:
“Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel mine inheritance.” That is the one verse they might run with: see, Egypt is his people and Assyria is his people, so the Egyptians and the Assyrians are saved too. No problem. Go over a few chapters and see where this Egypt and Assyria are.

“And it shall come to pass in that day, that the Lord shall beat off from the channel of the river unto the stream of Egypt, and ye shall be gathered one by one, O ye children of Israel.” Gathered one by one: who? The children of Israel.

“And it shall come to pass in that day, that the great trumpet shall be blown”: that is Christ coming. “And they shall come which were ready to perish in the land of Assyria, and the outcasts in the land of Egypt.” Earlier it said Egypt and Assyria; here it is the land of Assyria and the land of Egypt, and the ones coming out of them are the children of Israel. So who is “Egypt my people” and Assyria? Israelites.

“And shall worship the Lord in the holy mount at Jerusalem.” My people in Egypt and my people in Assyria means Israel in those lands, scattered there and gathered out one by one to worship at Jerusalem. That is how precepts work: you don't build a doctrine for another nation on one verse.

precepts.label: Isaiah 11:11
precepts.why:
Just in case Isaiah 27 is not enough, beat a dead horse. “And it shall come to pass in that day, that the Lord shall set his hand again the second time to recover the remnant of his people.” That is the same gathering we read in Isaiah 27.

From where? “Which shall be left, from Assyria”: my people. “And from Egypt”: Egypt, my people. “And from Pathros”: still Egypt, my people. “And from Cush, and from Elam”: Elam is Iran and Pakistan, my people. “And from Shinar”: Shinar is Iraq, my people. “And from Hamath”: Syria, my people. “And from the islands of the sea”: the islands, whether the Mediterranean or the Caribbean. That is his people.

It names Assyria and Egypt right there with the rest, and in every one of those places it is the remnant of his people that he recovers, not the nations of those lands. So when Isaiah 19 says “Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands”, it is speaking of Israel scattered in Egypt and Assyria, whom the Lord recovers the second time.

precepts.label: Zechariah 10:6-10
precepts.why:
One more, just in case. “And I will strengthen the house of Judah, and I will save the house of Joseph, and I will bring them again to place them.” Bring them again: that is the second time, the recovering of Isaiah 11. “For I have mercy upon them: and they shall be as though I had not cast them off”: as though they had never been in captivity. “For I am the Lord their God, and will hear them.”

“And they of Ephraim shall be like a mighty man, and their heart shall rejoice as through wine: yea, their children shall see it, and be glad.” “I will hiss for them, and gather them; for I have redeemed them.” Both Judah and Joseph, Judah and Ephraim: he will gather all twelve tribes. “And they shall increase as they have increased. And I will sow them among the people: and they shall remember me in far countries; and they shall live with their children, and turn again.”

“I will bring them again also out of the land of Egypt, and gather them out of Assyria.” Bring who again? All twelve tribes, out of Egypt and out of Assyria, the same as Isaiah 11:11. “And I will bring them into the land of Gilead and Lebanon; and place shall not be found for them.”

So what does “Egypt my people” and “Assyria the work of my hands” mean? It means Israel in those lands. That makes four scriptures, and there is no arguing with it. That is called precepts.

precepts.label: Psalms 69:21-23
precepts.why:
Isaiah says the word came to the rulers “that they might go, and fall backward, and be broken, and snared, and taken.” David shows the same snare. “They gave me also gall for my meat; and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.” This is a writing of David, but it is Christ speaking through David regarding himself on the cross.

“Let their table become a snare before them: and that which should have been for their welfare, let it become a trap.” Let the rulers' table be a snare. That is why Isaiah said they would be snared, trapped, broken and stumble.

“Let their eyes be darkened, that they see not”: let the eyes of the elders, the rulers, be darkened, whereunto they were appointed, so that they see not the Messiah standing in front of them. When he walked on the earth they said, that's not the guy, it can't be him. The rest of the verse: “and make their loins continually to shake.”

So the prophecy of Isaiah 28 is in reference to the elders, the leaders that ruled us. They hated God and they hated their people, and the words of God through the prophets were darkened to them.

precepts.label: Isaiah 8:13-15
precepts.why:
Isaiah 28 says they would “fall backward, and be broken, and snared, and taken.” Broken by what? By that stone of stumbling, that rock of offence. Isaiah 8 names it: “Sanctify the Lord of hosts himself; and let him be your fear, and let him be your dread. And he shall be for a sanctuary”. The same Lord shall be for a sanctuary, “but for a stone of stumbling and for a rock of offence to both the houses of Israel”, the southern and northern kingdom, “for a gin and for a snare to the inhabitants of Jerusalem.” A gin is a trap, a snare.

“And many among them shall stumble, and fall, and be broken, and be snared, and be taken.” Many among them means the rulers in Jerusalem. They stumbled, fell and were broken, as Psalm 69 said, and rejected the Messiah because they were evil, sinful and rebellious. That is who he is talking to: the elders, the builders, the rulers.

That stone is the “tried stone, a precious corner stone” Isaiah 28:16 lays in Zion, the same stone which the builders refused in Psalm 118. Peter quotes both Isaiah and David: “a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offence, even to them which stumble at the word, being disobedient: whereunto also they were appointed.” Them which stumble are the builders, the rulers, and the word is Christ, the same as the rock. Not all Israel refused him; the builders refused him. Appointed means they were predestined to reject him. Take good notes and tie these together: Isaiah 28, Isaiah 8, Psalm 118 and 1 Peter 2 are the same stone.

precepts.label: Psalms 2:1-2
precepts.why:
The rulers in Isaiah 28 said, “We have made a covenant with death, and with hell are we at agreement”. David shows who that covenant was with: “Why do the heathen rage, and the people imagine a vain thing?” The heathen rage, and the people, our people, imagine a vain thing.

“The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers take counsel together, against the Lord, and against his anointed”. They work together: the wicked elders and the heathen, against the Lord and against his anointed, his Son and his disciples.

So the covenant with death and hell is the rulers of Israel aligning themselves with the other nations, in an alliance with the heathen oppressors, even trying to save them. Back then the Pharisees, the scribes and the elders were in bed with Rome; in verse 19 they accepted Rome over Christ. Today it is the Christian pastors and your Black politicians in bed with America. That covenant “shall be disannulled”, and they shall be overthrown along with everybody else by Babylon.

precepts.label: Isaiah 29:10
precepts.why:
Isaiah 28 ends saying “it shall be a vexation only to understand the report.” The report is that Christ is the Messiah, the head of the corner (Isaiah 53:1), and they would not hear it because they were in darkness. Isaiah 29 shows that darkness: “Stay yourselves, and wonder; cry ye out, and cry: they are drunken, but not with wine; they stagger, but not with strong drink.”

“For the Lord hath poured out upon you the spirit of deep sleep, and hath closed your eyes”. That deep sleep goes back to them being in darkness, blinded. Closed your eyes: you can't see, you're blind.

“the prophets and your rulers, the seers hath he covered.” Today it is your priests and pastors, your politicians, your modern-day educators, conservatives and liberals. They are blind to the word and cannot see.

That is why the rulers could not see the stone laid in Zion. They were in darkness, and whereunto they were appointed, they stumbled at him.

precepts.label: Proverbs 16:27
precepts.why:
The first sign of a bitter brother is that he is easily offended; he will “make a man an offender for a word”. The next sign is that he holds grudges, the thing Leviticus 19:18 forbids: “Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people”. And he is always revisiting past wrongs.

Proverbs names him: “An ungodly man diggeth up evil”. That is the bitter brother digging up evil, the plumber brother, digging up old ish. As we say up in the States, he's digging it up like he's a plumber.

“and in his lips there is as a burning fire.” That is deceit, and he is always hating. That is the brother with the banana on his lips, the certified hater like Cain: I don't like that. That's you.

So the one who makes a man an offender for a word is the same one who keeps digging up the old things. He lacks forgiveness, as Sirach 28 showed, and he will not let the past rest. Brother, you are not in the right spirit.

precepts.label: Ecclesiasticus 20:22
precepts.why:
Another sign of bitterness is quiet resentment: they sit back and stew in silence. Sirach shows that brother: “There is that destroyeth his own soul through bashfulness”. He is the bitter bashful brother, brother BB.

“and by accepting of persons overthroweth himself.” He'll say, man, brother, everything good. Then he is told, brother, I need you to go do this, this and this, and he says, yes sir. The whole time he is thinking, I ain't feel like doing ish for that MF. He says yes sir to your face, and he has no intention in his heart of doing it.

That is the same bitter spirit as the one that makes a man an offender for a word, only hidden. The loud one digs up evil; the bashful one smiles and resents in silence. Either way he destroys his own soul, and he overthrows himself.

precepts.label: Tobit 1:1
precepts.why:
Sennacherib came against Hezekiah and mocked his God, and one angel of the Lord went forth and smote “in the camp of the Assyrians a hundred and fourscore and five thousand: and when they arose early in the morning, behold, they were all dead corpses.” One angel killed 185,000 soldiers in their sleep. Judah was saved without bow or sword, just as Hosea said. “So Sennacherib king of Assyria departed, and went and returned, and dwelt at Nineveh”, and his own sons smote him with the sword while he worshipped in the house of Nisroch his god. He went home pissed off, and Tobit shows what he did.

Tobit was “of the tribe of Nephthali”, led captive in the time of Enemessar, which is the Greek form of Shalmaneser the fifth, out of “Nephthali in Galilee above Aser.” He is northern kingdom, carried to Nineveh. “I Tobit have walked all the days of my life in the ways of truth and justice, and I did many almsdeeds to my brethren, and my nation, who came with me to Nineve, into the land of the Assyrians.”

“The most High gave me grace and favour before Enemessar, so that I was his purveyor”, overseeing the food and rations. When Enemessar died, Sennacherib his son reigned, the same Sennacherib that attacked Hezekiah and lost 185,000 men. Tobit “gave my bread to the hungry, and my clothes to the naked: and if I saw any of my nation dead, or cast about the walls of Nineve, I buried him.” Assyria was very brutal and vicious; they would take Israelites to the top of the walls and throw them off, and Tobit would bury his brothers broken in pieces on the ground.

“And if the king Sennacherib had slain any, when he was come, and fled from Judea, I buried them privily; for in his wrath he killed many.” Why did he flee from Judea? Because he lost 185,000 men. He was mad that he could not overthrow Judah, so out of anger he started killing Ephraim. When a Ninevite complained of Tobit to the king, his goods were forcibly taken away, and “there passed not five and fifty days, before two of his sons killed him”, the same death Isaiah 37:38 records.

Then Sarchedonus, Esarhaddon, reigned and appointed Achiacharus, Tobit's brother's son, over all his father's accounts, so Tobit gained standing again through his nephew. So Isaiah shows the angel saving Judah, and Tobit shows the other side of that same day: the northern kingdom in captivity in Nineveh, bearing Sennacherib's wrath, and a faithful Naphtalite burying his brethren.

precepts.label: Hebrews 1:9
precepts.why:
Christ told Peter to forgive seventy times seven, and Christ never put numbers out just to put them there. Seven represents completion, but what is seventy times seven? Daniel shows it: “Seventy weeks are determined upon thy people and upon thy holy city”. That is 490 years, from Persia to Christ, “to finish the transgression, and to make an end of sins, and to make reconciliation for iniquity, and to bring in everlasting righteousness, and to seal up the vision and prophecy, and to anoint the most Holy.”

Who is the most Holy that is anointed? Hebrews 1:9 explains it: “Thou hast loved righteousness, and hated iniquity; therefore God, even thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows.” That is talking about Christ. Where Daniel says “to anoint the most Holy”, that is Christ.

So the seventy weeks run “unto the Messiah the Prince”, which is Jesus Christ, and the reconciliation for iniquity and the end of sins come through him. The prophecy was 490 years, completing that perfection through Christ, because we needed that mercy. We couldn't sacrifice when we were enslaved under Babylon and Persia; we were always in captivity, going from one captivity to the next, so we needed Christ.

The apostles said it: “Him hath God exalted with his right hand to be a Prince and a Saviour, for to give repentance to Israel”. That is why he told Peter to forgive his brother seventy times seven: because he forgave us seventy times seven. He is that complete perfection. But don't take him for granted.

precepts.label: Luke 21:20
precepts.why:
“And after threescore and two weeks shall Messiah be cut off, but not for himself”: cut off for the children of Israel. “and the people of the prince that shall come shall destroy the city and the sanctuary”. That prince that shall come and destroy the sanctuary is Titus. “and the end thereof shall be with a flood, and unto the end of the war desolations are determined.” The flood is 70 AD, the destruction, and us being led away into captivity.

Christ spoke of that same desolation: “And when ye shall see Jerusalem compassed with armies, then know that the desolation thereof is nigh.” What armies? The Roman armies. That is what Daniel 9:26 is speaking of, the prince that shall come and destroy the city and the sanctuary.

Then Daniel 9:27: “in the midst of the week he shall cause the sacrifice and the oblation to cease”: the temple being destroyed. “and for the overspreading of abominations he shall make it desolate, even until the consummation”. The Roman armies around Jerusalem were the sign that the desolation determined in the seventy weeks was at hand.

So the 490 years end with Christ cut off for us and the desolation of the city by Titus. After that there was no sacrifice for us but Christ, and that is why his sacrifice is our only way through to perfection.

precepts.label: Ezekiel 37:22
precepts.why:
Hosea says, “Then shall the children of Judah and the children of Israel be gathered together, and appoint themselves one head”. The children of Judah are the nation; the children of Israel, the northern kingdom, are the company of nations. Gathered together means they become one, and the one head is Christ. You read the same thing from multiple prophets, and Ezekiel says it this way: “And I will make them one nation in the land upon the mountains of Israel; and one king shall be king to them all”. The one king is the one head.

“and they shall be no more two nations, neither shall they be divided into two kingdoms any more at all”: no more southern and northern. Remember, one of them was not a nation at all. Isaiah said, “within threescore and five years shall Ephraim be broken, that it be not a people.” Ephraim became Lo-ammi, not my people, Gentiles, heathen, uncircumcised, all the same. “Neither shall they defile themselves any more with their idols, nor with their detestable things”. They are brought back together, just as Hosea said.

Christ said the same out of his own mouth: “I lay down my life for the sheep. And other sheep I have, which are not of this fold”. This fold is Judah, because Christ is of Judah; the other sheep are the northern kingdom. “them also I must bring, and they shall hear my voice”: they hear through the teachings of Judah first. “and there shall be one fold, and one shepherd.” The one shepherd is Christ himself. He is quoting Hosea 1:10-11 and Ezekiel 37:22.

Even Caiaphas, who hated the Messiah, prophesied it: “that Jesus should die for that nation; And not for that nation only, but that also he should gather together in one the children of God that were scattered abroad.” Those scattered abroad are the strangers of 1 Peter 1, the northern kingdom. The builders were appointed to reject Christ so he would be killed, and by his death the northern kingdom would get the chance to repent and be redeemed back into the fold. That could not be done unless Christ died.

So the not my people of Hosea 1 are the strangers Peter wrote to, “Which in time past were not a people, but are now the people of God”. Christ gathers both kingdoms together as one nation under one king.

precepts.label: Hosea 1:10
precepts.why:
Hosea's children were for signs. His daughter Lo-ruhamah means no mercy: “I will no more have mercy upon the house of Israel; but I will utterly take them away”, which is Assyria overthrowing Ephraim so that it would be not a people. Then his son: “Call his name Lo–ammi: for ye are not my people, and I will not be your God.” When you are not God's people and he is not your God, what does that make you? A Gentile, a heathen, a stranger, a non-Israelite. Judah read this and said, good, the hell with Ephraim; they ain't his people no more, they're Gentiles, and we can't deal with them.

But Hosea goes straight on: “Yet the number of the children of Israel shall be as the sand of the sea, which cannot be measured nor numbered; and it shall come to pass, that in the place where it was said unto them, Ye are not my people, there it shall be said unto them, Ye are the sons of the living God.” When they were told they were Gentiles, it would be said to them, no, you are not Gentiles; you are God's people.

Judah forgot this. Judah said, you guys are Gentiles forever. But Hosea says eventually you have to come together again: “Then shall the children of Judah and the children of Israel be gathered together, and appoint themselves one head”. That one head is Christ, and they are delivered together, united as one. Chapter 2 says the same: “I will have mercy upon her that had not obtained mercy; and I will say to them which were not my people, Thou art my people; and they shall say, Thou art my God.” Judah just took a black highlighter and covered that part, because they were evil and stupid.

The same thing is in Chronicles. The northern kingdom was “without the true God, and without a teaching priest, and without law”, because Jeroboam set up idols in Dan and Shiloh so they would not go south to worship in Jerusalem. That is why they were called strangers: King Asa “gathered all Judah and Benjamin, and the strangers with them out of Ephraim and Manasseh, and out of Simeon: for they fell to him out of Israel in abundance, when they saw that the Lord his God was with him.” Whenever Judah was on point, Ephraim came in. The Lord always uses Judah to bring Ephraim back, and the strangers, the not my people, turn out to be the sons of the living God.

precepts.label: Baruch 4:1
precepts.why:
Hosea says of Israel that “they break out, and blood toucheth blood.” Baruch shows what breaking out is: “This is the book of the commandments of God, and the law that endureth for ever: all they that keep it shall come to life; but such as leave it shall die.” Such as leave the law, or break away from it, shall die. That is what they break out means.

So the sins Hosea lists, swearing, lying, killing, stealing and committing adultery, are a breaking away from the book of the commandments. Where the law is left, there is no truth, no mercy and no knowledge of God in the land, because truth is the application of God's laws, and the laws of God are not being taught or enforced.

And once they break out, blood toucheth blood: violence, hatred, killing against each other. The law endures for ever and keeping it is life; leaving it is death. The truth is the only thing we have to get up out of here. There is no plan B. Outside of this is death.

That is why the land mourns. If those same sins abide in the body, adultery, stealing, lying, swearing, not applying God's laws, hatred, violence, the congregation will not grow and will not flourish. As leaders we must teach the laws, hold people accountable to them, and be the example ourselves, so people can see there has to be a change in the way we move and how we think.

precepts.label: Amos 3:3
precepts.why:
“Can two walk together, except they be agreed?” That is the answer to the one who decides not to congregate with the body on the Sabbath, or to congregate partially, and then congregates with somebody that has been put out of the body. That is out of order, and it is sin.

The Sabbath is not negotiable: remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy. We cannot cook, we cannot buy, we cannot sell on the Lord's Sabbath day, and we must congregate, because it is a holy convocation. There is no way around that; you cannot decide not to do it. It is those small things, the application of God's laws, that separate us.

People do otherwise because we rationalise in our minds what we think is acceptable and what God will be all right with. God said, No, my commandments are straight; this is what I told you to do. Our biggest problem is trying to put our own thoughts in on how it should be done, but the Lord said, Your thoughts are not my thoughts. It is not hard. It only gets hard when we start to rationalise.

precepts.why:
Hosea ends with a promise: “he shall come unto us as the rain, as the latter and former rain unto the earth.” What is the analogy of the former and latter rain? It's going to be a blessing. When we harvested crops, we looked forward to the rain coming. We needed the rain to come. When it didn't rain, we knew the Lord wasn't dealing with us. That's how he punished us.

We read that in Deuteronomy 28: “And thy heaven that is over thy head shall be brass, and the earth that is under thee shall be iron. The Lord shall make the rain of thy land powder and dust: from heaven shall it come down upon thee, until thou be destroyed.” That is what it looks like when the rain does not come: the heaven shut like brass, the ground hard as iron, and powder and dust in place of rain.

So when Hosea says the Lord will come unto us as the rain, it is the curse being lifted. “Come, and let us return unto the Lord: for he hath torn, and he will heal us”. We were torn by captivity and slavery, and he will heal us, meaning redeem us out of this situation. After two days, two thousand years, he revives us, and in the third day he raises us up to who we are, to our identity.

“Then shall we know, if we follow on to know the Lord”: if we follow on to apply what God tells us to do, then shall we be bound up and healed. The rain the Lord withheld in the curses comes back as a blessing, and that blessing will be in the application of his laws.

precepts.label: Jeremiah 7:12
precepts.why:
Amos warns Ephraim, “seek not Beth–el, nor enter into Gilgal”, for “Beth–el shall come to nought.” These were places built for worship by Abraham and Jacob, and Ephraim turned them into seats of idolatry. So Gilgal would surely go into captivity, and Beth–el would be destroyed. “Seek the Lord, and ye shall live; lest he break out like fire in the house of Joseph”: the house of Joseph is Ephraim.

Jeremiah turns the same judgment on Judah: “But go ye now unto my place which was in Shiloh, where I set my name at the first, and see what I did to it for the wickedness of my people Israel.” Go look at Shiloh and see what I did to it. “I spake unto you, rising up early and speaking, but ye heard not; and I called you, but ye answered not”: they refused the prophets.

“Therefore will I do unto this house, which is called by my name, wherein ye trust, and unto the place which I gave to you and to your fathers, as I have done to Shiloh. And I will cast you out of my sight, as I have cast out all your brethren, even the whole seed of Ephraim.” What was done to Ephraim will be done to Judah: the heathen come in, destroy the sanctuary and lead them captive. The exact same way. The same thing happens to both houses, both kingdoms. He raised up Assyria to overthrow Ephraim, and he raised up Babylon to overthrow Judah.

And they would not hear it. Amaziah the priest of Bethel, one of the low-level priests raised up that was not Levi, told Amos, “go, flee thee away into the land of Judah, and there eat bread, and prophesy there: But prophesy not again any more at Beth–el: for it is the king’s chapel”. Go teach Judah; you are disturbing the king's church. Amos was blitzing the churches. But the Lord said to him, “Go, prophesy unto my people Israel.” The Lord always sent his prophets to his people, and his people alone, to repent. It is the same with Jacob today: the one preaching the word of God is called a troublemaker.

So Bethel came to nought as Shiloh did, and Israel went “into captivity forth of his land”: their wives made harlots, their sons and daughters fallen by the sword, their land divided by line as it is to this day, dying “in a polluted land”. That began with the northern kingdom, but eventually it happened to all of us as a whole.

precepts.label: John 1:29
precepts.why:
We did not return to what the Most High commanded, the feasts he told us to go back to, and that is why we were in need of a saviour, an ultimate sacrifice. From Abraham to David, from David to the carrying away into Babylon, and from Babylon to Christ were fourteen generations each; we were always in slavery.

“And she shall bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins.” His name means he saves. His people: the Israelites only. From their sins. That is why he was the ultimate sacrifice.

His cousin John expounds on it: “Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world.” The Lamb of God. Christ was that perfect, ultimate sacrifice, the lamb that takes away the sins of the people he came to save.

precepts.label: Hebrews 10:5-8
precepts.why:
To expound further on Christ being the ultimate sacrifice: “Wherefore when he cometh into the world, he saith, Sacrifice and offering thou wouldest not, but a body hast thou prepared me”. The body was Christ. The sacrificial laws of animal sacrifice were a preparation for what was to come, a shadow of good things to come; the good thing that came was the body of Jesus Christ, dying only for the nation of Israel.

“In burnt offerings and sacrifices for sin thou hast had no pleasure.” The Most High had no pleasure in those sacrifices. They were temporary, to train us and prepare us for Christ.

“Then said I, Lo, I come (in the volume of the book it is written of me,) to do thy will, O God.” In the volume of the book: the whole book, not just the New Testament. Christ is present in the Old Testament, and Christ is present before the Old Testament.

“Above when he said, Sacrifice and offering and burnt offerings and offering for sin thou wouldest not, neither hadst pleasure therein; which are offered by the law”. So the offerings of the law pointed to the body prepared for him, the one sacrifice that saves his people from their sins.

precepts.label: John 1:3
precepts.why:
Christ was always the plan. He is the author, the executive producer, whatever title you want to give him. From before the Old Testament, the body prepared for him in the volume of the book was the plan for saving his people from their sins.

John shows it: “All things were made by him”. All things were made by Christ: the principalities, the things you see out in space, the worlds, with an s. “And without him was not any thing made that was made.”

The one who made all things is the one who came as the Lamb of God to save his people. The sacrifices of the law, the seventh day and the rest it points to were all his from the beginning. So when the angel said “thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins”, it was the Maker of all things coming to fulfil the plan that was always his.

precepts.label: Matthew 23:1-3
precepts.why:
Christ said, “Take heed and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and of the Sadducees.” What was the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees? Matthew 23 shows the first part of it.

“The scribes and the Pharisees sit in Moses’ seat: All therefore whatsoever they bid you observe, that observe and do; but do not ye after their works: for they say, and do not.” They were hypocrites. What they said out of Moses' seat was the law, and that you do. But their works did not match their words.

“Do not ye after their works”, because their works were after someone else, and that is the rest of the leaven: who their works followed. The Passover reminds us that we were delivered because we were unleavened, righteous; so to be delivered again we have to move in the same spirit and purge the leaven out, not just check the box on the physical bread.

precepts.label: Mark 8:15
precepts.why:
Christ warned in Matthew 16 to beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, and in Matthew 23 he said to do what they bid from Moses' seat, but not after their works. Whose works were they following? Mark tells it: “And he charged them, saying, Take heed, beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, and of the leaven of Herod.”

The leaven of Herod. That lets you know whose manner they were following: they were following the white man, Esau. That is why he tells us to beware.

So their leaven was not just being hypocrites. They were following after the manner of the wicked. Leaven is an influence that spreads, and when the rulers of Israel took on Herod's leaven, it spread through them; they came to move in the same spirit as the wicked they served. That is the warning to us: do not take on the leaven of Herod, the spirit of Esau, while wearing the garments of Israel.

precepts.label: John 11:45-48
precepts.why:
John 11 shows the leaven of the Pharisees and of Herod at work. “Then many of the Jews which came to Mary, and had seen the things which Jesus did, believed on him.” They believed on Christ.

“But some of them went their ways to the Pharisees, and told them what things Jesus had done.” Wherever there is good, evil has to be there. You had the believers, and then you had coons set up there, running to tell.

“Then gathered the chief priests and the Pharisees a council, and said, What do we? for this man doeth many miracles. If we let him thus alone, all men will believe on him: and the Romans shall come and take away both our place and nation.” The Romans. That lets you know who their masters were and who they were following after. That is the leaven of Herod.

Leaven is an influence that spreads. That bitterness is on the inside, and it corrupts the spirit, the same bitterness that was in Cain toward Abel. The scribes and Pharisees were bitter toward Christ and wanted him dead to keep their place under Rome. If you are bitter toward your brother, you are in the same position as the scribes and Pharisees: the same spirit.
