precepts.label: Romans 13:8-10
precepts.why:
James 2:8 says “If ye fulfil the royal law according to the scripture, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself, ye do well.” What is the royal law? Romans 13 lays it out.

“Owe no man any thing, but to love one another: for he that loveth another hath fulfilled the law.” What law? Love your neighbour as yourself. “For this, Thou shalt not commit adultery, Thou shalt not kill, Thou shalt not steal, Thou shalt not bear false witness, Thou shalt not covet”: every one of those is the royal law. “And if there be any other commandment”, any other commandment regarding your neighbour outside of those, “it is briefly comprehended in this saying, namely, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.”

Love your neighbour as yourself is an abbreviation of the six commandments. Of the ten spoken commandments, the first four are how you observe God, and the last six are how you serve your neighbour: honour your father and mother, don’t commit adultery, don’t kill, don’t steal, don’t bear false witness, don’t covet. Those six are briefly comprehended in that one saying. The ten spoken commandments were themselves an abbreviation.

“Love worketh no ill to his neighbour”: no ill like being a respecter of persons, seating the man with the gold ring in a good place and telling the poor man to stand over there. “Therefore love is the fulfilling of the law.” Do we keep it? Yes, you simple Christians. That is the royal law James is talking about, and respect of persons is sin against it.

precepts.label: Matthew 22:34-40
precepts.why:
“But when the Pharisees had heard that he had put the Sadducees to silence, they were gathered together.” Christ had put the Sadducees to shame, and the Pharisees saw how sharp he was. “Then one of them, which was a lawyer, asked him a question, tempting him.”

A lawyer is a scribe. Their job was writing the Bible over and over again, because ink fades and animal skin and paper rip and smear, so it had to be copied again and again. They were the recorders and copyists, and they knew the law and the prophets off top. That is why he was tempting Christ: he already knew the answer. “Master, which is the great commandment in the law?”

“Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind. This is the first and great commandment.” That is the first four of the ten spoken commandments. “And the second is like unto it, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.” That is the six, the royal law of James 2:8.

“On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets.” These two are an abbreviation of all the laws. Loving God with all your heart, soul and mind means keeping the Sabbath day holy, the Passover, Tabernacles, Pentecost, the new moons, keeping the congregation, and the dietary law: don’t drink blood, don’t eat pork or shrimp. That is all serving God. The ten are an umbrella over all of them.

precepts.label: Mark 12:28-33
precepts.why:
Mark gives the same account with more detail, and it ties into sacrifice. “And one of the scribes came.” In Matthew he is called a lawyer; in Mark he is called a scribe, because they wrote things over and over and had the law in their minds. There were a bunch of them, but he was bold and spoke up: “Which is the first commandment of all?”

“The first of all the commandments is, Hear, O Israel; The Lord our God is one Lord”: that is Deuteronomy 6:4. “And thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind, and with all thy strength: this is the first commandment.” The commandments, the dietary law, the civil law, the sacrificial law, all of that is in there. “And the second is like, namely this, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. There is none other commandment greater than these.” If you can keep those, you can keep them all.

“Well, Master, thou hast said the truth”: true, true, true. Then verse 33: “to love him with all the heart, and with all the understanding, and with all the soul, and with all the strength, and to love his neighbour as himself, is more than all whole burnt offerings and sacrifices.” It is better than sacrifices. That is why Mark is loved: he makes it clear.

Why is it more than sacrifices? Because Israel would mess around, offer sacrifices, and then hate their neighbour, kill their neighbour, steal from their neighbour, bang their neighbour’s wife or sleep with their neighbour’s husband, but offer the best animal. The Lord said, I don’t care about that stuff. I care about your obedience, loving each other, loving me above the animals.

precepts.label: Sirach 35:1-3
precepts.why:
Mark 12:33 said loving God and your neighbour is more than all whole burnt offerings and sacrifices. Ecclesiasticus 35 says the same.

“He that keepeth the law bringeth offerings enough: he that taketh heed to the commandment offereth a peace offering.” Keeping the law is offering enough.

“He that requiteth a good turn offereth fine flour.” Under the offerings, you offered an animal, or fine flour if you were poor. Here, requiting a good turn, which is loving your neighbour as yourself, is the fine flour. “And he that giveth alms sacrificeth praise.”

“To depart from wickedness is a thing pleasing to the Lord; and to forsake unrighteousness is a propitiation.” Propitiation means mercy, reconciliation. Departing from wickedness toward your neighbour is what reconciles you to God, which is why the royal law of James 2:8 stands above the sacrifices.

precepts.label: 1 Samuel 15:22
precepts.why:
Saul disobeyed a direct order, and through Samuel the Lord asks him a question: “Hath the Lord as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the Lord?” Answer it.

“Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams.” The Lord cared about obedience more than animal sacrifices.

That is the same point as Mark 12:33, that loving God and your neighbour “is more than all whole burnt offerings and sacrifices.” Saul wanted to bring the sacrifice after he had disobeyed; Israel wanted to bring the best animal after they had wronged their neighbour. The Lord wants the obedience. And that is why James 2 holds us to the royal law, love thy neighbour as thyself, and not to an offering that covers over a sin against the brother.

precepts.label: Psalms 40:6
precepts.why:
“Sacrifice and offering thou didst not desire; mine ears hast thou opened: burnt offering and sin offering hast thou not required.” This is quoted again in Hebrews 10.

David is saying, you opened my ears, and I understand the spirit: you don’t really care about sacrifices. Remember David wanted to build the temple. But the spirit was revealed to him that the sacrifices were just a placeholder for Christ to show up. He learned that because Christ was speaking through him.

So David realized: you don’t care about sacrifices at all, you care about obedience. That is what Samuel told Saul when he was king, “to obey is better than sacrifice.” And it is why the royal law of James 2, loving the neighbour and not being a respecter of persons, is what God is looking for.

precepts.label: Proverbs 21:3
precepts.why:
“To do justice and judgment is more acceptable to the Lord than sacrifice.”

To do justice and judgment, just like the Lord told Saul to do, is more acceptable than sacrifice. He says it over and over and over again: in Samuel, in the Psalms, in Mark, and here in Proverbs.

Justice and judgment is how you treat your neighbour. In James 2 the assembly seated the rich man in a good place and told the poor man to stand there, and James asks, “Are ye not then partial in yourselves, and are become judges of evil thoughts?” That is the opposite of doing justice and judgment, and no sacrifice would make up for it. Keeping the royal law is what is acceptable to the Lord.

precepts.label: Hosea 6:5-6
precepts.why:
“Therefore have I hewed them by the prophets; I have slain them by the words of my mouth.” The word of God can slay; it is the spirit. “And thy judgments are as the light that goeth forth.”

“For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.” He was not about the sacrifice. That was a schoolmaster, a placeholder. He desired mercy and the knowledge of God.

The Lord eventually said away with it, through the prophets themselves. And that is where James 2:13 lands: “For he shall have judgment without mercy, that hath shewed no mercy; and mercy rejoiceth against judgment.” You shall receive no mercy if you show no mercy. Mercy rejoices against judgment: the Most High chooses to have mercy rather than to judge you for violating the royal law, and he looks for that same mercy in us toward our neighbour.

precepts.label: Judith 16:16
precepts.why:
“For all sacrifice is too little for a sweet savour unto thee, and all the fat is not sufficient for thy burnt offering: but he that feareth the Lord is great at all times.”

All sacrifice is too little. He that fears the Lord is great at all times. The Lord is saying, sacrificing, I don’t care about that; fearing me and obeying me is more important.

That closes the line of scriptures: Mark 12:33, Ecclesiasticus 35, 1 Samuel 15:22, Psalms 40:6, Proverbs 21:3, Hosea 6:6 and Judith 16:16 all say the same thing. Then back to James 2. “For whosoever shall keep the whole law, and yet offend in one point, he is guilty of all.” Christians use this to say that if you sin in one law you break them all, so you can’t keep them at all. But the context is the royal law, love your neighbour as yourself, and James explains it himself: “For he that said, Do not commit adultery, said also, Do not kill.” If you commit no adultery but you kill your brother, you are a transgressor of the royal law.

“So speak ye, and so do, as they that shall be judged by the law of liberty.” Under the old covenant, if you violated the moral law, moved your neighbour’s landmark or slept with your brother’s wife, you got death. Christ redeemed us from that and put us under the law of liberty. So stop doing it.

classes.title: Navigating Through Paul's Letters: Works Of The Law & Liberty

precepts.label: 2 Esdras 9:7
precepts.why:
“Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone.” People say the law can’t save you, you are not justified by the works of the law. Ezra answers it: “And every one that shall be saved, and shall be able to escape by his works, and by faith, whereby ye have believed.”

Everyone that shall be saved shall escape by what? His works. And by faith. Works and faith go hand in hand; you have to have both, as James said. You will be saved by both: not faith alone and no works, not faith and no commandments, not commandments and no faith. That makes no sense; it is dead, being alone.

“though a man say he hath faith, and have not works? can faith save him?” That is like a man saying I got a paycheck, with no job. I get paid tomorrow. You got a job? No. It is the dumbest thing you can say out of your mouth. Your faith proves your works and your works prove your faith. Abraham had faith and kept the commandments of God, and his keeping the commandments proved his faith.

And it goes back to the royal law, loving your neighbour as yourself. Telling a brother with no food and no clothes “be ye warmed and filled”, and giving him nothing, makes no damn sense. Even so, faith without works makes no sense: the faith does not exist.

precepts.label: Revelation 14:12
precepts.why:
“shew me thy faith without thy works, and I will shew thee my faith by my works.” You cannot show faith without works. You show your faith through your actions, which is keeping the commandments of God. John says it in Revelation: “Here is the patience of the saints: here are they that keep the commandments of God, and the faith of Jesus.”

Keep the commandments, and the faith of Jesus. The faith is one, and the commandments are the works. That is what James said, and what Ezra said: saved by works and by faith.

“Thou believest that there is one God; thou doest well: the devils also believe, and tremble.” Even the devils, the unclean spirits, believe in God and are afraid of him. “But wilt thou know, O vain man, that faith without works is dead?” The vain man is the Christianity follower: faith without works, Calvinism, Protestantism, Catholicism. The saints are marked by both, the commandments of God and the faith of Jesus, and one without the other is dead.

precepts.label: Revelation 22:14
precepts.why:
The saints “keep the commandments of God, and the faith of Jesus”, and Revelation shows what the commandments are for: “Blessed are they that do his commandments, that they may have right to the tree of life, and may enter in through the gates into the city.”

That do his commandments: deeds, actions, works. They must do the commandments to enter in through the gates, and have faith in Christ. They go hand in hand.

That is James’ point: “Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone.” A man who says he has faith but does no works, who will not keep the commandments, has no right to the tree of life. Christ redeemed us from the death that came from breaking the law, and put us under the law of liberty, “So speak ye, and so do, as they that shall be judged by the law of liberty.” The doing is what gives the right to enter the city.

precepts.label: Romans 4:3
precepts.why:
“Was not Abraham our father justified by works, when he had offered Isaac his son upon the altar?” Abraham was justified by his works because his works proved his faith. Offering Isaac was his action. “Seest thou how faith wrought with his works, and by works was faith made perfect?” His faith was perfected by his works; he was proven faithful by them.

“And the scripture was fulfilled which saith, Abraham believed God, and it was imputed unto him for righteousness.” That is the scripture Paul quotes in Romans 4: “Abraham believed God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness.” The same belief Paul speaks of is the belief James says was fulfilled when Abraham laid his son on the altar. His belief was counted for righteousness, and his works showed that belief to be real, “and he was called the Friend of God.”

So Paul and James do not disagree. “Ye see then how that by works a man is justified, and not by faith only”, which goes back to Romans 2:13, that the doers of the law shall be justified. Abraham believed, and kept the commandments of God, and both went together.

precepts.label: Galatians 3:6
precepts.why:
James says “the scripture was fulfilled which saith, Abraham believed God, and it was imputed unto him for righteousness: and he was called the Friend of God.” Paul quotes the same scripture to the Galatians: “Even as Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him for righteousness.”

Abraham’s belief was accounted for righteousness, and James shows how it was fulfilled: when he offered Isaac his son upon the altar. “Seest thou how faith wrought with his works, and by works was faith made perfect?” Faith worked together with his actions, and his actions perfected it.

“Ye see then how that by works a man is justified, and not by faith only.” Rahab the harlot was justified the same way. She believed that if she helped the spies escape, they would spare her life; that was her faith, and receiving the messengers and sending them out another way was her works. “For as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead also.” We have to keep the commandments and the faith of Christ; each goes with the other.

precepts.label: Isaiah 45:4
precepts.why:
Peter writes “to the strangers scattered throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia”, and calls them “Elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father”. Who are the elect? Isaiah answers it: “For Jacob my servant’s sake, and Israel mine elect, I have even called thee by thy name”. Israel mine elect, or my chosen, same thing. So the strangers Peter is writing to are Israelites. They are the grafted in strangers, the ones called not a people, not my people, the northern kingdom.

The thought does not change in chapter 2; he is not writing to somebody else. “But ye are a chosen generation”: the “ye” is the strangers of chapter 1 verse 1, the elect of verse 2. Chosen goes back to elect. They are “a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people”, and all Israel is a peculiar people. Context matters. Against them stand “them which be disobedient”, the builders, the southern kingdom's Pharisees, Sadducees, scribes, elders and rulers, who stumbled at the stone and were appointed to it, so Christ could be killed and die for both kingdoms, to reunite all twelve tribes. That could not be done unless Christ died.

Peter is quoting Hosea. Jezreel is the seed of Israel, and God says “I will sow her unto me in the earth; and I will have mercy upon her that had not obtained mercy; and I will say to them which were not my people, Thou art my people”. So Peter writes “Which in time past were not a people, but are now the people of God”. That promise was made to the northern kingdom in Isaiah 7 and 8 and Hosea 1. When Christ dies he redeems them back into being his people and gathers them together in one. How could you find that out if you don't know your history?

thread.text: Wherefore also it is contained in the scripture, Behold, I lay in Sion a chief corner stone, elect, precious: and he that believeth on him shall not be confounded.

precepts.label: Hosea 2:22-23
precepts.why:
“And the earth shall hear the corn, and the wine, and the oil; and they shall hear Jezreel.” Jezreel is the seed of Israel. This is chapter 2 of the same context as Hosea 1:10-11, read earlier, where God gathers them together again and they appoint themselves one head.

“And I will sow her unto me in the earth”: I will bring her, adopt her back unto me in the earth. Then, “and I will have mercy upon her that had not obtained mercy; and I will say to them which were not my people, Thou art my people; and they shall say, Thou art my God.” Which were not my people, or not a people. That promise was made to the northern kingdom, in Isaiah 7 and 8 and in Hosea 1.

Now go back to Peter. He is writing to the strangers scattered throughout Pontus, Galatia and the rest, the elect according to the foreknowledge of God, and he says “Which in time past were not a people, but are now the people of God: which had not obtained mercy, but now have obtained mercy.” Sound familiar? Peter is quoting Hosea. When Christ dies he redeems them back into being his people and gathers them together in one.

The builders who stumbled were appointed to it: by rejecting Christ they had him killed, and by his being killed the northern kingdom was granted a chance to repent and be redeemed back into the fold. Israelites that are not studying never see this. How could you find that out if you don't know your history?

thread.text: But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light:

precepts.label: 1 Peter 1:1
precepts.why:
Peter writes “to the strangers scattered throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia”, and verse 2 calls them “Elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, through sanctification of the Spirit, unto obedience and sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ”. These strangers are the same strangers that came to keep the Passover in Chronicles, and the elect is the same name given to those called according to Hosea and Isaiah in Romans 9. Who's that? Israel.

So when verse 9 says “But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people”, the “ye” is these same strangers scattered abroad. They are set against “them which be disobedient”: the builders that disallowed the stone, the southern kingdom, the Pharisees that rejected Christ and stumbled at that stone of stumbling and rock of offence of Isaiah 8:14. They were “appointed” to it. They had to put Christ to death, and his death gave the other kingdom the chance to repent and come back into the fold. By rejecting Christ they brought back in the same brothers they rejected.

The scattered elect were called “out of darkness into his marvellous light”, which is Isaiah 9:1. And they are the ones “Which in time past were not a people, but are now the people of God: which had not obtained mercy, but now have obtained mercy.” That goes back to Deuteronomy 32 and Isaiah 7, not a people. The northern tribes, cast off and scattered, are now the people of God.

precepts.label: Zechariah 11:8
precepts.why:
Peter describes men that “despise government” and “are not afraid to speak evil of dignities”, men with “eyes full of adultery”, “beguiling unstable souls”, with hearts “exercised with covetous practices”. “These are wells without water”, no understanding, “clouds that are carried with a tempest”, friends with this one, over there with that one, “to whom the mist of darkness is reserved for ever.” That same darkness is reserved for you when you hate your brother, and that is why they are confounded about Cornelius and Romans 11.

Zechariah shows the same kind of rulers in Christ's day: “Three shepherds also I cut off in one month”. The three shepherds are the Pharisees, the Sadducees and the scribes, the rulers, the builders. The Romans killed them. He says “my soul lothed them”: I hated them. And “their soul also abhorred me”: they hated me then.

So the evil speakers of 2 Peter 2 are the same spirit as the three shepherds: rulers who hated Christ and hated their own brothers, and God loathed them and cut them off. The dudes out here right now are doing the same thing they were doing back then, and that is how you will discover them.

precepts.label: Isaiah 6:9-10
precepts.why:
The mist of darkness is reserved for those who speak evil of dignities and hate their brothers. Isaiah shows where that darkness comes from: “Go, and tell this people, Hear ye indeed, but understand not; and see ye indeed, but perceive not. Make the heart of this people fat, and make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes”. Shut their eyes: darkness.

Why? “lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and convert, and be healed.” Convert means repent. Lest they repent. The Lord shuts the eyes of the builders, the rulers, so they cannot see.

That is why Peter calls them “wells without water”, with no understanding. When you badmouth Peter, Paul, John the Baptist or any of the apostles and prophets, the Lord puts the spirit of darkness on you until you become a borderline, if not full-blown, Christianity teacher. Your ears are made heavy and your eyes are shut, and you cannot understand even the basic verses. Be mindful how you deal with brothers; brothers who murmur and speak evil bug out and go back into the world.

precepts.label: Matthew 15:14
precepts.why:
Christ said of the Pharisees: “Let them alone: they be blind leaders of the blind.” Leave them alone. “And if the blind lead the blind, both shall fall into the ditch”: snared and trapped.

In Matthew 23 Christ cursed them out the whole chapter: “Woe unto you, ye blind guides”. Keep that in mind: blinded, blind, eyes darkened, eyes shut. They say whosoever swears by the temple it is nothing, but whosoever swears by the gold of the temple is a debtor: they worry about money, hearts “exercised with covetous practices” as Peter says. “Ye fools and blind: for whether is greater, the gold, or the temple that sanctifieth the gold?”

The same blind leaders are around today, dark clothes, a dark spirit. That is why we do not come together with other camps: different doctrines, and some of those doctrines can lead you to damnation. Leaders of other camps who show up at our schools unannounced and then throw a tantrum on video for views show their real color. We don't show up at your house unannounced; there are channels, and you call first. A GMS member sat in one of our schools for months living a double life. We pray brothers get it right, but we let the blind leaders alone and keep doing the work.

precepts.label: John 8:44-48
precepts.why:
“Ye are of your father the devil, and the lusts of your father ye will do. He was a murderer from the beginning, and abode not in the truth, because there is no truth in him.” Christ is speaking to the elders, the rulers. “When he speaketh a lie, he speaketh of his own: for he is a liar, and the father of it.”

“And because I tell you the truth, ye believe me not.” “He that is of God heareth God’s words: ye therefore hear them not, because ye are not of God.” You elders of Satan.

Then watch the next verse: “Then answered the Jews, and said unto him, Say we not well that thou art a Samaritan, and hast a devil?” They called Christ a Samaritan because they hated the northern kingdom. Samaritan was a derogatory term to them: you're a Samaritan and a devil. Meanwhile they were planning to kill him. That's how evil and conniving they were.

This is the dividing hatred, and it is the same spirit Peter describes: evil speakers, not afraid to speak evil of dignities, heirs of that mist of darkness. The rulers of the south hated their northern brothers so much that the name of the north was their insult, and the same hatred of brothers is still found today.

precepts.label: 2 Corinthians 3:13-16
precepts.why:
“And not as Moses, which put a vail over his face, that the children of Israel could not stedfastly look to the end of that which is abolished”. Moses spent time with the Lord, and the Lord's glory was upon him so that he was blinding; he had to wear a vail. The shine on Moses represented the new covenant: the glory of Christ was on Moses, and the people could not look at Moses just as they could not see Christ in the Old Testament.

“But their minds were blinded”. Not their eyes; their minds. How is your mind blinded? You read the Bible and say, I don't see it, when it is right there. Nations can't be saved: I don't see it. Israelite: I don't see it. Then, “for until this day remaineth the same vail untaken away in the reading of the old testament; which vail is done away in Christ.” When it comes to reading the Old Testament, they are still blinded as they were with Moses, blinded to Christ and to the northern kingdom being brought back in.

“But even unto this day, when Moses is read, the vail is upon their heart”: they don't understand the prophets. “Nevertheless when it shall turn to the Lord, the vail shall be taken away”: when they repent, they will see Christ. “Now the Lord is that Spirit: and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty”, liberty from keeping animal sacrifice.

That is the mist of darkness Peter speaks of, and the only way out of it is turning to the Lord. Keep God's commandments and laws; it works for us.

classes.title: The Dividing Hatred: the Grafted in Strangers

precepts.label: 1 John 4:20-21
precepts.why:
John says it again in his fourth chapter: “If a man say, I love God, and hateth his brother, he is a liar: for he that loveth not his brother whom he hath seen, how can he love God whom he hath not seen?” And: “this commandment have we from him, That he who loveth God love his brother also.”

You can't love one and hate the other. It is impossible. If you love your brother, by default you love God; if you love God, by default you love your brother. They go hand in hand: God and people, God and race. What the white man promotes among his people is what we should promote among ourselves. When we say it, we're called racist; when they say it, they're patriots.

That is the light and darkness of 1 John 2. “He that saith he is in the light, and hateth his brother, is in darkness even until now.” Picture our people in captivity, while the ones who enslaved us rule. For hundreds of years they spent billions, even trillions, to hide our history from us. They tortured us, beat us, raped us, castrated us, and broke us physically, mentally, psychologically and spiritually. Their ruling is their heaven; we are in hell. And an Israelite in that hell spends himself teaching the heathen the access he has to our heaven. That is hate. You hate your people and you hate yourself, and for that you are in darkness.

Esau does not forget. He holds grudges: when they took Maduro, rumor has it they bombed the mausoleum where Hugo Chavez is buried, because Chavez spoke ill of America. But Jacob forgets, even in the midst of captivity. The man who says he loves God while caring more for his oppressor than for his own brother is, in John's own word, a liar.

precepts.label: John 13:34-35
precepts.why:
Where did John get this “new commandment”? From Christ: “A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another; as I have loved you, that ye also love one another. By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another.”

Christ said it to the disciples, and John repeated it in his epistle. Christ said it over and over again: “These things I command you, that ye love one another.”

That is why John can say in the same breath, “I write no new commandment unto you, but an old commandment which ye had from the beginning”, and then, “Again, a new commandment I write unto you”. It is old because it came from Moses' time. It is called new because Israel was not following it. Going back to Moses, we were children in whom is no faith, rebellious; we waxed fat and kicked.

So the mark of Christ's disciples is love one to another, among our own people. “He that loveth his brother abideth in the light, and there is none occasion of stumbling in him.” The one who despises his brother and his people will stumble, and stumble in a lot of deep but basic things.

precepts.label: Mark 12:28-31
precepts.why:
Normally Matthew 22 is read for this, but Mark is heavy. A scribe asked, “Which is the first commandment of all?” “And Jesus answered him, The first of all the commandments is, Hear, O Israel; The Lord our God is one Lord: And thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind, and with all thy strength: this is the first commandment. And the second is like, namely this, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. There is none other commandment greater than these.”

There is none greater, because if you love your brother as yourself you can keep all the commandments; they all go hand in hand. You cannot love God and hate your brother. By loving God you will love your brother, and by loving your brother you love God.

What Christ is really saying is: love your people, love your ways. Why would the Most High give us these laws? Because we had learned how to hate one another, and the law was given to teach us. The same laws we give to our people today: love your ways, love your people, love your neighbour.

Think how brainwashed you are in this captivity if, like Deacon Nathan was saying earlier, you are in captivity and care more about your oppressor than your own kind. Your people are being oppressed and all you care about is your oppressor: you're a dummy, and that is the kindest word for it. That is the darkness that “hath blinded his eyes.”

precepts.label: Leviticus 19:17-18
precepts.why:
Christ isn't saying anything new. He calls it a new commandment, but we heard it before, in the law: “Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thine heart: thou shalt in any wise rebuke thy neighbour, and not suffer sin upon him. Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the Lord.”

Your neighbour is your people. Your neighbour is your brother. Love your neighbour as yourself. When you despise yourself, you despise your God that resembles you and your brother that resembles you. It is a domino effect. You can't love one and hate the other.

That is what John means: “Brethren, I write no new commandment unto you, but an old commandment which ye had from the beginning.” It was there from Moses' time. And it is the very hatred Moses warned against in the beginning, when we were all together, that divided Ephraim and Judah. They began to despise each other, and that is why both fell: the northern kingdom first, and the southern kingdom afterward.

So “he that hateth his brother is in darkness, and walketh in darkness, and knoweth not whither he goeth”. Christ's new commandment was already in the law, and Israel's fall came from not keeping it.

precepts.label: Hebrews 12:1
precepts.why:
The Lord says to them who keep his commandments and precepts, “let not your sins weigh you down.” Sin feels good. The pleasure comes, and once the pleasure is gone the guilt rolls in, and you feel like crap. After a while it becomes a burden, and it shows on you. Many of us came into the school guilty of things too shameful to confess, and some are still doing them. When you come forward and confess, you feel that weight lifted off: thank God.

Paul uses the same picture: “Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us.” Lay aside every weight. Your sins of character are weights.

If you run a race carrying weights, can you run fast? No. You can still be in the race, but you either keep adding weight until you come in last and never cross the finish line, or you take the weights off. One weight off and you feel lighter; another off and you are faster. You were in third, now second, now first.

Some of y’all say, I’m good back here, I’ll just walk. Meanwhile you are on a timer, and time at the end is running out. A race is won by the time you run. If you are walking in a race, you are not winning at all, by no account.

That is why we lay aside every weight: the sins that so easily beset us are what hold us back. It is what 2 Esdras means: do not let your sins weigh you down.

precepts.label: Sirach 19:20
precepts.why:
Sirach 15:15 says, “If thou wilt, to keep the commandments, and to perform acceptable faithfulness.” Keeping God's commandments is performing acceptable faithfulness: those are your actions, and that is where your faith lies. Your works prove your faith and your faith proves your works; they go hand in hand. God “hath set fire and water before thee: stretch forth thy hand unto whether thou wilt.”

For anyone still confused, Sirach 19:20 says it again: “The fear of the Lord is all wisdom; and in all wisdom is the performance of the law, and the knowledge of his omnipotency.” The performance of the law is the acceptable faithfulness of Sirach 15. Wisdom is not only knowing the law; it is performing it.

The words “the knowledge of his omnipotency” mean knowing that God is all around us, and we acknowledge it by keeping his laws.

This is what Habakkuk and Paul mean by the just living by faith. Paul says “the law is holy, and the commandment holy, and just, and good.” The just are those who keep God's laws and commandments, and they live by faith in Christ. Fearing God, keeping his law and living by faith are one walk.

precepts.label: Genesis 26:5
precepts.why:
God told Isaac why the promise stood: “Because that Abraham obeyed my voice, and kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws.” Abraham obeyed, and he kept the charge, the commandments, the statutes and the laws. That is past tense. It tells you what Abraham was doing from the beginning that proved his faith. His obedience was his acceptable faithfulness, the performance of Sirach 15:15.

Paul writes, “And the law is not of faith: but, The man that doeth them shall live in them.” The law meant there is the law of sacrifice, which came later. Abraham's faith came first, and his faith and the promise to him go hand in hand; the promise predates the law of sacrifice.

“Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us”. The curse of the law is condemnation, not being able to atone for every sin. Caiaphas pointed it out without knowing it: “it is expedient for us, that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation perish not.” Both the northern and southern kingdoms were under the old covenant they agreed to in Deuteronomy 27 and kept breaking, so both were condemned and destroyed by the nations. But the Lord loved them, sent his son to die for them, and took them out of that contract into a new one, “That the blessing of Abraham might come on the Gentiles through Jesus Christ”, meaning the northern kingdom.

Paul says “before faith came, we were kept under the law”, and “the law was our schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ, that we might be justified by faith.” The schoolmaster is the law of sacrifice, and the “we” is Israel. After faith came, “we are no longer under a schoolmaster.” Jews, Greeks, bond, free, male and female were all the same people of God in Christ.

“And if ye be Christ’s, then are ye Abraham’s seed, and heirs according to the promise.” Abraham is the father of faith, so his children should be children of faith like him: keeping the commandments the way he did, with faith in Christ instead of the animal sacrifice the Galatians were bewitched back into. The promise pertains to the Israelites, not to all nations.

precepts.label: Proverbs 21:16
precepts.why:
Baruch says the law “endureth for ever: all they that keep it shall come to life; but such as leave it shall die.” Since the beginning of time this law has been in place. Break it and judgments come upon you; keep it and blessings come upon you. Solomon shows what happens to those who leave it: “The man that wandereth out of the way of understanding shall remain in the congregation of the dead.”

Look at your old pictures and old videos from when you were in the world. You look dead, spiritually dead. Run down and tired, twenty-one years old looking forty, when that was supposed to be the pinnacle of life, of your youth. We wandered out of the way of understanding, and we were like the walking dead. That is why the law is called a spirit: the commandments are spirit, and without them there is no life in us.

They make those movies mocking us. We were the congregation of the dead. And it is ironic that zombies walk groping. That is groping at noonday, what the Lord said would come on us for breaking his commandments: walking around trying to catch on to something, gravitate to something, all confused in the spirit. Even with the sun at its apex we could not see. We were blinded. We were distracted.

So the law is the difference between the living and the dead. Those who keep it come to life, the way we did when we came into this truth; those who wander from it remain in the congregation of the dead.

precepts.label: Romans 7:12
precepts.why:
Manasseh prays, “Thou therefore, O Lord, that art the God of the just, hast not appointed repentance to the just.” Obviously: if you are just, you have nothing to repent from. But what makes you just?

Paul answers it: “Wherefore the law is holy, and the commandment holy, and just, and good.” The law is holy, and the commandment is holy, just and good. When you are applying it, that is what makes you just. That is what makes you good: the law and the commandment.

So the God of the just is the God of those who keep the commandments, “as to Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, which have not sinned against thee.” They kept God’s laws. Repentance was not appointed for them.

“But thou hast appointed repentance unto me that am a sinner.” Manasseh knew he was not just. He had broken the holy, just and good commandment on every count, and his only hope was the repentance the Lord appoints unto sinners.

precepts.label: 1 Timothy 1:9-11
precepts.why:
Manasseh says the God of the just “hast not appointed repentance to the just.” Paul says the same exact thing: “Knowing this, that the law is not made for a righteous man, but for the lawless and disobedient.” The law is not made for a righteous man, just as repentance is not appointed for the just.

It is made “for the ungodly and for sinners, for unholy and profane, for murderers of fathers and murderers of mothers, for manslayers, For whoremongers, for them that defile themselves with mankind”, that is homosexuality, “for menstealers”, child traffickers, “for liars, for perjured persons”, liars under oath before the judge, “and if there be any other thing that is contrary to sound doctrine”, anything not listed.

“According to the glorious gospel of the blessed God, which was committed to my trust.” The law is in accordance with the gospel. You cannot have one without the other.

That list is Manasseh. Under the law of Moses he was condemned on all accounts: he killed babies, he was an idolater and a murderer, he shed the blood of children from one end of Jerusalem to the other, and he was steeped in every evil. He was America, but a king; Epstein, but a king; King Diddy Manasseh. There was no animal he could sacrifice. He was a king worthy of death, and his mindset was, I’m the king, I do what I want. The Lord said, you’re the king? Cool, and threw him in prison.

Yet the Lord appointed repentance unto him, and let him live as an example to us in this time. Most kings and celebrities with that status will not repent. When you are rich you become your own god; they literally call them idols. Oprah said on air she does not respect a jealous God. But Manasseh humbled himself, and that is the lesson.

precepts.why:
Manasseh prays, “I am not worthy to behold and see the height of heaven for the multitude of mine iniquities.” Many of us think this. Christ gives a parable about that very man, spoken “unto certain which trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and despised others.” Those who were righteous in their own eyes and despised everybody else were the Pharisees: I'm more righteous than you, you're wicked.

“Two men went up into the temple to pray; the one a Pharisee, and the other a publican.” The publican was a tax collector, and they were praying in the same place. The Pharisee thanked God he was “not as other men are, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even as this publican”, not like this dude next to him, and bragged, “I fast twice in the week, I give tithes of all that I possess.”

“And the publican, standing afar off, would not lift up so much as his eyes unto heaven.” Why? Because he felt unworthy, the same as Manasseh, who could not behold the height of heaven. He “smote upon his breast, saying, God be merciful to me a sinner”: the same thing Manasseh said in his prayer, my sins are a multitude.

Christ's judgment: “this man went down to his house justified rather than the other.” The sinner who asked for mercy went home justified; the one who called himself righteous did not. “for every one that exalteth himself shall be abased”: that is what Manasseh did in the beginning, exalting himself, and he was brought down to a low condition, locked up and imprisoned. “and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted”: that is Manasseh later on, after he humbled himself.

So humble yourself and you will be exalted. Exalt yourself and you will be humbled, and you are not going to like that humbling either.

precepts.label: Psalms 40:8
precepts.why:
Manasseh confesses, “I did not thy will, neither kept I thy commandments.” Those two go together, because the Lord's will is his commandments. David shows it: “I delight to do thy will, O my God: yea, thy law is within my heart.”

To do God's will is to have his law in your heart. The laws of God are the will of God; God's will is his laws. So when Manasseh says he did not God's will, he is saying the same thing twice: he did not keep the commandments. Not doing the will of God is not some mystery feeling; it is breaking his law.

That is why Manasseh goes straight on to say, “I have set up abominations, and have multiplied offences.” He had provoked the Lord's wrath and done evil before him, and he was bowed down with iron bands, locked up with no release. A man who delights to do God's will keeps the law within his heart; Manasseh had to come to that by being humbled, bowing the knee of his heart and acknowledging his iniquity.

precepts.label: 2 Peter 2:4-17
precepts.why:
Manasseh begs, “forgive me, O Lord, forgive me, and destroy me not with mine iniquites. Be not angry with me for ever, by reserving evil for me.” What does he mean by reserving evil for you? There is evil reserved for you while you keep playing around. Peter shows it.

“For if God spared not the angels that sinned, but cast them down to hell, and delivered them into chains of darkness, to be reserved unto judgment.” These are the angels that fell in Adam’s time, cast down to destruction. Remember David said, take not thy holy spirit from me. If the Lord removes his Holy Spirit from you, you are now in chains of darkness, reserved unto judgment.

“The Lord knoweth how to deliver the godly out of temptations, and to reserve the unjust unto the day of judgment to be punished.” Manasseh said, don’t reserve evil for me, because the Lord reserves punishment for the unjust. “But chiefly them that walk after the flesh in the lust of uncleanness, and despise government. Presumptuous are they, selfwilled, they are not afraid to speak evil of dignities.” Chiefly means primarily. Despising government is despising leadership. When leadership is trying to help you and you say, nah, I know what I’m doing, you are not humble. Your heart is arrogant.

They follow “the way of Balaam the son of Bosor, who loved the wages of unrighteousness”: money. “These are wells without water, clouds that are carried with a tempest”, carried about by different doctrines, all over the place, “to whom the mist of darkness is reserved for ever.” The mist of darkness is the reprobate mind; the Holy Spirit is not in them. That is evil reserved for them.

So Manasseh, a king worthy of that very judgment, humbled himself and asked the Lord not to reserve that evil for him. We must do the same while repentance is open.

precepts.label: 2 Peter 3:7
precepts.why:
Manasseh prays, “Be not angry with me for ever, by reserving evil for me; neither condemn me to the lower parts of the earth.” Peter shows the great evil reserved at the end: “But the heavens and the earth, which are now, by the same word are kept in store, reserved unto fire against the day of judgment and perdition of ungodly men.”

The heavens and the earth are reserved unto fire: nuclear fire, and the hellfire that follows after it. That is what the ungodly are reserved for, and that is what Manasseh was asking not to be reserved for him. The lower parts of the earth he speaks of go into the hellfire again.

Then he says, “For thou art the God, even the God of them that repent.” He is the God of them that repent. Unto them that repent he grants return. So humble yourself before you are sick, examine yourself before judgment, and in the time of sins show repentance, because the fire is already reserved for the ungodly.

thread.label: Prayer of Manasseh 1:13
thread.text: and in me thou wilt shew all thy goodness: for thou wilt save me, that am unworthy, according to thy great mercy.

classes.title: The Mercy and Humility of King Manasseh

precepts.label: Sirach 17:24
precepts.why:
Manasseh prays, “For thou art the God, even the God of them that repent; and in me thou wilt shew all thy goodness: for thou wilt save me, that am unworthy, according to thy great mercy.” He is the God of them that repent.

Sirach shows what he does for them: “But unto them that repent, he granted them return, and comforted those that failed in patience.” Unto them that repent he grants return, return to the land. And he comforts those who failed in patience.

That is the goodness Manasseh expected God to show in him. He was unworthy, a king condemned on every count, but he repented, and the Lord brought him back again to Jerusalem into his kingdom. So it is for Israel as a nation: Manasseh is the living embodiment of the nation, and if we repent, he grants us return.

precepts.label: Sirach 18:20-21
precepts.why:
Manasseh humbled himself in his affliction, and the Lord saved him, unworthy as he was, “according to thy great mercy.” Sirach tells us to do it before the day comes: “Before judgment examine thyself, and in the day of visitation thou shalt find mercy.”

Before judgment, examine yourself, and in the day of visitation you will find grace and mercy. “Humble thyself before thou be sick, and in the time of sins shew repentance.”

Manasseh waited until he was bound in fetters in Babylon before he humbled himself. Don’t wait until you are sick, locked up, or exposed. In the time of wrong, show repentance, and the same mercy Manasseh found will be there for you.

precepts.label: Matthew 3:2-8
precepts.why:
The Lord is “the God of them that repent”, and repentance is the first thing preached when the kingdom draws near: “Repent ye: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.” It was the first thing Christ said in his preaching, and it goes for all of us.

John the Baptist cried it: “For this is he that was spoken of by the prophet Esaias, saying, The voice of one crying in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make his paths straight.” He wore “raiment of camel’s hair, and a leathern girdle about his loins; and his meat was locusts and wild honey.” And “Jerusalem, and all Judea, and all the region round about Jordan” came out and were baptized of him in Jordan, “confessing their sins.”

“But when he saw many of the Pharisees and Sadducees come to his baptism, he said unto them, O generation of vipers, who hath warned you to flee from the wrath to come?” What are you doing here? “Bring forth therefore fruits meet for repentance”: fruits suitable for repentance.

That is the fig tree in Luke 13, dunged and dug about so that it may bring forth fruit. That was John’s ministry, paving the way for Christ. Manasseh did not only say sorry; he confessed his sins and his life changed. That is repentance with fruit.

precepts.label: Matthew 9:11-13
precepts.why:
Manasseh says, “thou wilt save me, that am unworthy, according to thy great mercy.” Christ came for exactly such as him. “And when the Pharisees saw it, they said unto his disciples, Why eateth your Master with publicans and sinners?” It is the same spirit as the Pharisee in Luke 18: I’m more righteous than this publican over here.

“But when Jesus heard that, he said unto them, They that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick.” That is exactly what Manasseh said: the just need no repentance. The sick are the ones the law is made for, the lawless and the whoremongers.

“But go ye and learn what that meaneth”: go learn what that means, you guys are stupid. “I will have mercy, and not sacrifice.” He is quoting Hosea. God cares about mercy more than sacrifice. “For I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.”

God is the God of those that repent. Manasseh had no sacrifice that could cover him under the law, but he found mercy, because Christ came to call sinners like him to repentance.

precepts.label: Hosea 6:6
precepts.why:
When the Pharisees asked why Christ ate with publicans and sinners, he told them, “But go ye and learn what that meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice.” He was quoting Hosea: “For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.”

God doesn’t care about sacrifice the way the Pharisees did. He cares about mercy. He desires mercy, and the knowledge of God, more than burnt offerings.

That is why Manasseh could be saved. Under the law there was no animal he could sacrifice to cover what he had done; he was finished. But the Lord desired mercy and not sacrifice, and so Manasseh could pray, “in me thou wilt shew all thy goodness: for thou wilt save me, that am unworthy, according to thy great mercy.”
